lessons.title: Start here · Your Testing with Generative AI preparation route
lessons.summary: Understand the CT-GenAI exam, its weighted K3 questions and how to keep mock papers fresh.

blocks.text: This independent English study pack is aligned to the ISTQB Certified Tester Testing with Generative AI (CT-GenAI) syllabus v1.1, dated 2026-04-27. It is not an official exam or an accredited training course. Version 1.1 is a minor update of v1.0: it corrects and clarifies selected sections (for example 'context manipulation' replaces 'data exfiltration' as an attack vector, and section 4.1.3 now introduces AI assistants with goal-driven, agent-based test automation) without changing the structure, learning objectives or scope. CT-GenAI is about using generative AI (GenAI) to support software testing; testing AI-based systems is the subject of the separate CT-AI certification. The ISTQB Foundation Level (CTFL) certificate is required before taking the exam, so the lessons assume Foundation terms such as test basis, test condition, test analysis, test design and test monitoring.

blocks.title: Exam format
blocks.text: The full simulation has 40 questions, 60 minutes and 46 available points: 8 K1 and 26 K2 questions worth one point each, and 6 K3 questions worth two points each. The K3 questions apply GenAI to test analysis (GenAI-2.2.1), test design and implementation (2.2.2), automated regression testing (2.2.3), test monitoring and control (2.2.4), choosing prompting techniques (2.2.5) and identifying hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases (3.1.2). The pass mark is 30 points (65%). Select-TWO questions need exactly two answers and give nothing for a partial answer. The 75-minute version models the 25% extension for non-native-language candidates; your exam provider decides eligibility.

blocks.title: A practical route
blocks.text: First pass: read the lessons in order, including each 'Syllabus details to know' block, and solve the self-checks before reading their solutions. Chapter 2 carries 16 of the 46 points, so give prompt engineering the most time. Second pass: practise the hands-on guides with any chatbot you are allowed to use at work, using only non-sensitive data. Third pass: take paper A under timed conditions, review each wrong answer and each guess, revisit the linked lesson, then take papers B to D on separate days.

blocks.title: Fresh evidence
blocks.text: The four papers contain different questions and share no question families. The 75-minute version of a paper repeats its questions. Learning sessions and 20-question short practice draw from the whole bank, including paper questions, so they can use up a paper's freshness. LearnForge's readiness rule needs strictly more than 90% on each of three full mocks with fresh families, so keep at least three papers unopened until you want to measure readiness. A simulated pass (30 of 46 points) is reported separately.

blocks.title: How the chapters fit together
blocks.text: Chapter 1 explains what GenAI and large language models (LLMs) are, how tokens, embeddings and context windows work, the kinds of LLMs, multimodal models, what LLMs can do for testing and how testers interact with them. Chapter 2 is the practical core: the six-part prompt structure, prompt chaining, few-shot and meta prompting, system and user prompts, applying GenAI to each test activity, and evaluating and refining prompts. Chapter 3 covers the risks: hallucinations, reasoning errors, biases, non-determinism, data privacy and security, energy use and regulation. Chapter 4 describes LLM-powered test infrastructure: architecture, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agents, fine-tuning and LLMOps. Chapter 5 covers organisational adoption: shadow AI, strategy, model selection, adoption phases, skills and changing roles.

blocks.title: Read beyond the objective list

lessons.title: 1.1 · GenAI foundations: LLMs, tokens and model types
lessons.summary: Recall the AI spectrum, explain how LLMs work, distinguish foundation, instruction-tuned and reasoning LLMs, and use multimodal models.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text:
Generative AI uses large pre-trained models to generate human-like output such as text, images or code. The AI spectrum: symbolic AI represents knowledge with symbols and logical rules to mimic human decision-making; classical machine learning (ML) is data-driven and needs data preparation, feature selection and model training (for example to categorise defects or predict software problems); deep learning uses neural networks that learn features automatically from very large, complex datasets such as images, audio or text, although humans may still annotate data, tune models or validate results; GenAI uses deep learning to create new content by learning and mimicking patterns in training data. The key advantage of GenAI for testing is that pre-trained models can be applied directly to test tasks without an additional training phase, which brings its own risks.

LLMs are based on the generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) model and trained on very large datasets such as books, articles and websites. Small language models (SLMs) have fewer parameters and offer lightweight, focused solutions. Tokenization breaks text into tokens (a character, a sub-word or a word); embeddings turn tokens into vectors in a high-dimensional space so that tokens with similar meaning or role sit close together. The transformer processes long text sequences and learns how tokens relate; at inference it predicts the next token. Output is statistically plausible, but plausible is not necessarily correct. LLMs are non-deterministic because inference is probabilistic and depends on hyperparameter settings, so the same input can give different outputs. The context window is the amount of preceding text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider; a larger window keeps coherence over long material such as test logs, but increases computational complexity and processing time.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester pastes a 120-page log into a chatbot and asks for the first failing test. The answer refers to a test that appears near the end of the log and misses an earlier failure. Explanation: the log may exceed the context window, so the beginning was not considered, and the next-token prediction produced a plausible but incomplete answer. Better approach: split the log, or ask for a summary per section and verify each against the raw log.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Tokens are not always words: a token can be a character, a sub-word or a word. Embeddings are numerical vectors, not the original text. A larger context window is not free: it increases computation and processing time. Plausible LLM output is not evidence of correctness.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which approach on the AI spectrum would a rule engine that flags a defect report as 'critical' whenever it contains 'data loss' belong to? Solution: symbolic AI, because it uses explicit symbols and rules. A model trained on 10,000 labelled defect reports to predict severity is classical ML (or deep learning, if it uses deep neural networks that learn features automatically).

blocks.title: LLM types and multimodal models
blocks.text:
Foundation LLMs are general-purpose models trained on vast, diverse datasets (text, code, images and other modalities); they are flexible but usually need adaptation for specific tasks. Instruction-tuned LLMs are derived from foundation models and fine-tuned on datasets that pair prompts with expected responses, improving instruction following, task adherence and coherence. Reasoning LLMs extend instruction-tuned models with structured abilities such as logical inference, multi-step problem solving and chain-of-thought reasoning, so they suit high-cognitive-load tasks. Testing uses both instruction-tuned (non-reasoning) and reasoning LLMs, depending on how much reasoning the task needs.

Multimodal LLMs process several modalities (text, images, sound, video); tokenization is adapted for each, for example images are converted into embeddings by vision-language models before the transformer processes them. Vision-language models integrate visual and textual information for image captioning, visual question answering and checking consistency between text and images. In testing they can analyse screenshots and GUI wireframes together with defect reports or user stories, find discrepancies between expected results and what a screenshot shows, and generate test cases that combine textual and visual cues.

blocks.title: Worked case: a screenshot and a user story
blocks.text: A tester uploads a checkout screenshot and the user story 'As a shopper I can apply one voucher per order; the total updates immediately'. The prompt asks a multimodal LLM to list differences between the story and the screen. The model notices two voucher fields on the screenshot and a total that does not change after a voucher is shown as applied. The tester confirms both observations manually before raising defects, because the model can misread images.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Choose the most suitable model type for each task: (1) rewriting a test report summary in a more formal tone; (2) working out an execution order for 40 test cases with dependencies, priorities and environment constraints; (3) comparing a wireframe image with acceptance criteria; (4) a generic model to be adapted later with organisation data.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) An instruction-tuned LLM is enough: it follows instructions well and the task needs little reasoning. (2) A reasoning LLM, because the task needs multi-step problem solving; verify the result anyway. (3) A multimodal LLM with vision-language capability. (4) A foundation LLM, which is general-purpose and usually adapted further.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-1.1.2 and HO-1.1.4)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Use a tokenizer tool on a test case description, a stack trace and a table of test data, and compare the token counts; note how punctuation and identifiers split. Then write a prompt that gives a multimodal LLM both a screenshot and a user story and asks for discrepancies; review the inputs first, run the prompt, and verify every claim in the response against the screenshot.

lessons.title: 1.2 · LLM capabilities for testing and ways to interact
lessons.summary: Give examples of LLM capabilities across the test process and compare AI chatbots with LLM-powered testing applications.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: LLMs excel at processing natural language and code, generating coherent text and code, answering questions, summarising, translating and, when multimodal, analysing images. They can interpret requirements, specifications, screenshots, code, test cases and defect reports. Key capabilities for test tasks: requirements analysis and improvement (find ambiguities, inconsistencies or missing information in the test basis and suggest clarifying questions for stakeholders); test case creation support (generate test cases and suggest test objectives from requirements or user stories); test oracle generation (help generate expected results); test data generation (datasets, boundary values, combinations); test automation support (generate test scripts from test case descriptions, improve existing scripts, suggest test techniques); test result analysis (summaries, classifying anomalies by severity and priority); and testware creation (test plans, test reports, defect reports, kept updated as the project evolves).

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A team asks an LLM to read a new requirement: 'The system shall lock the account after several failed logins.' The LLM points out that 'several' is ambiguous, that the lock duration and unlock procedure are missing, and suggests questions for the product owner. This is requirements analysis and improvement. It then proposes boundary values (2, 3 and 4 failed attempts once the number is agreed), which is test data generation.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: An AI chatbot and an LLM-powered testing application can use the same LLM; what differs is how you interact with it and how it is integrated. Chatbots are conversational and interactive; LLM-powered testing applications integrate LLM capabilities through APIs into tools to perform well-defined, often automated tasks. Strong prompt engineering is needed in both cases.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Classify: (1) a tester asks a chatbot to explain pairwise testing to a new colleague; (2) a test management tool calls an LLM API every night to cluster new defect reports; (3) a tester iteratively refines a set of exploratory test ideas in a conversation. Solution: (1) chatbot, onboarding and quick knowledge access; (2) LLM-powered testing application, automated and integrated; (3) chatbot, using prompt chaining for iterative refinement.

blocks.title: AI chatbots versus LLM-powered testing applications
blocks.text: AI chatbots provide a user-friendly conversational interface to LLMs. Testers enter questions, commands or prompts and get immediate, context-aware responses; with prompt chaining they can refine results iteratively. Chatbots suit routine tasks, exploratory testing, fast feedback, clarifying test concepts, exploring requirements and potential test cases, and onboarding new testers; their intuitive interface also suits non-technical stakeholders and encourages adoption. LLM-powered testing applications integrate LLM capabilities through APIs to perform well-defined and often automated tasks. They offer more customisation and scalability, let organisations and tool vendors embed GenAI in existing test frameworks, and automate repetitive or complex tasks such as test case generation, defect analysis or test data synthesis. Advanced implementations create AI agents that perform particular testing roles (chapter 4). Either way, carefully designed prompts with clear, specific instructions improve accuracy, relevance and alignment with test objectives.

blocks.title: Worked case: choosing an interaction model
blocks.text: A bank's test team needs 50,000 synthetic, privacy-preserving customer records every sprint in a fixed format for its regression environment. A chatbot would need manual copying and would not scale; an LLM-powered testing application that calls the model through an API, applies a fixed prompt template and writes the records into the test data store fits better. For an analyst exploring a new loan regulation and brainstorming test ideas, a chatbot conversation is more suitable.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Name the LLM capability used in each case: (1) suggest the expected discount for a basket of 3 items under a stated rule; (2) produce a Selenium script from a written test case; (3) summarise last night's 1,200 test results and group failures by likely cause; (4) keep the test plan aligned with new sprint goals.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Test oracle generation (expected results). (2) Test automation support (scripts from test case descriptions). (3) Test result analysis (summaries and classification of anomalies). (4) Testware creation and maintenance (test plans kept up to date).

lessons.title: 2.1 · Effective prompts: structure, techniques, system and user prompts
lessons.summary: Give examples of the six prompt components, differentiate prompt chaining, few-shot and meta prompting, and distinguish system from user prompts.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A structured prompt for software testing typically has six components. Role: the perspective or persona the model should adopt, such as tester, test manager or test automation engineer, which shapes its responsibilities and tone. Context: background the model needs to determine test conditions, such as the test object, the functionality to test and relevant circumstances. Instruction: clear, imperative, concise directives describing the task and its requirements. Input data: the information needed to do the task, such as user stories, acceptance criteria, screenshots, code, existing test cases or output examples; detailed and structured input improves accuracy. Constraints: restrictions or special considerations, which specify how instructions are applied to the input data. Output format: the expected format, structure or characteristics of the response. Combine this structure with a prompting technique suited to the task and the LLM.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Role: 'You are a senior test analyst for a payments product.' Context: 'We are testing the refund feature of release 4.2 for card payments in the EU.' Instruction: 'Derive test conditions from the acceptance criteria below.' Input data: three acceptance criteria. Constraints: 'Cover only the criteria provided; do not invent features; use equivalence partitioning for amounts.' Output format: 'Return a markdown table with columns ID, condition, criterion reference, priority.'

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Constraints say how the instruction is applied (for example scope limits or rules to respect); output format says what the answer must look like (for example a table with named columns). A line such as 'present the defects in a table with columns ID, severity and description' belongs to output format, not to constraints or instructions.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Classify these prompt lines: (1) 'Act as a test automation engineer'; (2) 'Use only keywords from the attached keyword library'; (3) 'Here is the user story: …'; (4) 'Generate Gherkin scenarios'; (5) 'Answer as JSON with fields title and steps'. Solution: (1) role; (2) constraint; (3) input data; (4) instruction; (5) output format.

blocks.title: Core techniques; system and user prompts
blocks.text:
Three core prompting techniques are commonly combined with the six-component structure. Prompt chaining breaks a task into intermediate steps across multiple prompts; each result is checked (manually or automatically) and refined before the next step, which improves accuracy and suits complicated test tasks needing decomposition and systematic checks of intermediate output. Few-shot prompting includes several examples in the prompt; zero-shot prompting has no example and relies on pre-existing knowledge, and one-shot prompting has a single example. Examples give the model a clear reference and make results consistent; few-shot prompting suits tasks where examples illustrate the required behavior. Meta prompting uses the LLM to generate or refine prompts in an iterative cycle evaluated by the tester; it reduces manual prompt-design effort, helps when the tester is unsure how to write a prompt, and is a form of pairing between tester and AI. The techniques can be combined.

The system prompt is usually defined by the developer or tester, is typically not visible or editable by the chatbot's user, and acts as a predefined command set that defines the LLM's behavior, personality and operational parameters (formal tone, concise answers, domain rules, behaviors to avoid). It stays constant for the session and may contain the role, context, constraints and general output instructions. The user prompt is the actual input from the user; it changes with each interaction, is visible, and forms the immediate context for each response. The model responds using both together. System prompts should be clear and specific about role and constraints; user prompts should be focused and well structured with explicit instructions, context and output format.

blocks.title: Worked case: a reusable test-review assistant
blocks.text: A team sets a system prompt: 'You are a test reviewer aligned with ISTQB terminology. Be concise, never invent requirements, and flag uncertainty explicitly.' Each tester then sends user prompts such as 'Review these five test cases against acceptance criterion AC-3 and list gaps as bullet points.' The system prompt keeps behavior consistent across the team; the user prompts carry the task-specific instructions and input data.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Identify the technique: (1) 'Here are two examples of a user story with its Gherkin scenarios; now write scenarios for this third story'; (2) 'First list ambiguities in the story. [check] Next evaluate testability of each criterion. [check] Then propose improved criteria'; (3) 'Write the best prompt I should use to generate boundary value test cases for an age field'; (4) 'Generate test conditions for this story' with no examples.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Few-shot prompting (two examples; one example would be one-shot). (2) Prompt chaining with human verification between steps. (3) Meta prompting: the LLM generates the prompt that the tester evaluates and refines. (4) Zero-shot prompting.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-2.1.1, HO-2.1.2a, HO-2.1.2b)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Take three prompts you have used at work and mark each part as role, context, instruction, input data, constraints or output format; add the missing parts and compare the results. Then rewrite one task three ways (prompt chain, one-shot or few-shot, and meta prompt) and note which produced the most accurate and complete output.

lessons.title: 2.2 (part 1) · Applying GenAI to test analysis, design and implementation
lessons.summary: Apply GenAI to test analysis tasks (K3) and to test design and implementation tasks (K3).

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: GenAI can support test analysis by generating and prioritising test conditions, identifying defects in the test basis and providing coverage analysis. Inputs include requirements, user stories, technical specifications and GUI wireframes; outputs are typical analysis work products such as prioritised test conditions (for example acceptance criteria). Typical tasks: identify potential defects in the test basis (inconsistencies, ambiguities, incomplete information, using similar requirement patterns or past defect reports); generate test conditions by breaking requirements into measurable, testable statements; prioritise test conditions by risk when likelihood and impact are provided, considering regulatory compliance, user-facing features such as login or payment, and historical defect data; support coverage analysis by mapping requirements and stories to test conditions to find gaps; and suggest test techniques, such as boundary value analysis or equivalence partitioning, suited to the requirement. The quality and relevance of the inputs directly affect the accuracy and precision of the output.

blocks.title: Worked example (applying prompt chaining to test analysis)
blocks.text: Task: a stable, already reviewed set of requirements for a parking app must be turned into prioritised test conditions with a coverage check. Chain: step 1, give the requirements and ask for test conditions; verify them. Step 2, give the verified conditions plus risk likelihood and impact for each feature and ask for a risk-based priority; verify. Step 3, give the prioritised conditions and the requirements and ask which requirement aspects are not covered; verify. A single prompt asking for 'prioritised, complete test conditions' would skip the checks between steps. Asking for ambiguity detection first would be redundant here because the requirements were already reviewed.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Applying GenAI does not mean accepting its output. In K3 scenarios, the best answer keeps a human verification step, provides the inputs the task needs (for example risk information before asking for risk-based prioritisation), and uses the technique that fits the task. Watch for options that ask the LLM to do something it has no input for.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A tester wants risk-based priorities for 30 test conditions but gives the LLM only the conditions. What is missing? Solution: information on risk likelihood and impact (and, where relevant, regulatory, user-facing and historical defect factors). Without it, the model would invent priorities.

blocks.title: Test design and implementation
blocks.text: Test design elaborates and refines test conditions into test cases and other testware; test implementation creates or acquires the testware needed to run tests. GenAI can support: test case generation (draft test cases from functional and non-functional requirements, with preconditions, inputs, expected results and coverage criteria, from basic functional checks to complex end-to-end tests); test data synthesis (representative, privacy-preserving synthetic data resembling production, including extreme situations and varied conditions, without exposing sensitive information); automated test script generation (manual test procedures and automated scripts from structured test cases, compatible with automation frameworks, and updated for new requirements); and test execution scheduling and prioritisation (analyse test cases and dependencies to optimise schedules by priority, risk, resources and objectives).

blocks.title: Worked case: Gherkin with few-shot prompting
blocks.text: A team writes all acceptance tests in Gherkin. The tester's prompt contains a role, the context (online library loans), an instruction ('write Given-When-Then scenarios for the new user story'), two examples each pairing a story, its test conditions and its scenarios (few-shot), constraints ('one scenario per condition; use the domain glossary terms'), and the output format ('valid Gherkin, Feature header, no commentary'). The results are reviewed; where a scenario is wrong, the examples or the prompt are refined.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: You must prioritise 25 regression test cases for tonight's run. Some depend on others (for example 'create account' before 'close account'), and each has a risk rating. Design a prompt chain for this test implementation task and say where human verification happens.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Step 1: give the test cases and dependencies; ask the LLM to list dependency chains; verify them. Step 2: give the verified chains plus risk ratings and ask for an order that respects dependencies and runs high-risk cases first; verify that no dependency is broken. Step 3: ask for an execution schedule that fits the time window and resources; check it manually. Reasoning errors are likely in multi-criteria prioritisation, so each intermediate result needs a check.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-2.2.1a, HO-2.2.1b, HO-2.2.2a-c)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Use a wireframe image plus a user story in a structured multimodal prompt to generate acceptance criteria; then refine criteria with a chain (ambiguities, then testability, then completeness), correcting each step. Generate functional test cases from acceptance criteria, ask for a coverage table, and use a meta prompt to design an end-to-end test procedure. Use few-shot prompting for Gherkin scenarios and a prompt chain for test case prioritisation with dependencies.

blocks.text:
Test analysis tasks (2.2.1): identify potential defects in the test basis; generate test conditions from the test basis; prioritise test conditions by risk level (likelihood and impact; regulatory compliance, user-facing features, historical defect data); support coverage analysis (map requirements and stories to test conditions); suggest test techniques. Inputs: requirements, user stories, technical specifications, GUI wireframes. Output quality depends on input quality and relevance.
Test design and implementation tasks (2.2.2): test case generation; test data synthesis (representative, privacy-preserving synthetic data); automated test script generation; test execution scheduling and prioritisation (dependencies, priority, risks, resources, objectives).

lessons.title: 2.2 (part 2) · Regression testing, monitoring and choosing techniques
lessons.summary: Apply GenAI to automated regression testing (K3), test monitoring and control (K3) and select prompting techniques for a context (K3).

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Regression suites grow with each release and run frequently in CI/CD pipelines, so they are strong automation candidates. GenAI can help create, maintain and optimise automated regression suites and, by performing impact analysis on code changes, focus regression effort where it is most needed. Typical activities: implementing test scripts with keyword-driven automation (mapping predefined keywords for common test steps to test cases and generating scripts); impact analysis and test optimisation (analyse code changes to find high-risk areas and target regression tests); self-healing and adaptive tests (adjust scripts automatically for minor UI or API changes so suites stay stable); automated test reporting and insights (detailed, timely reports, dashboards, trends and predictive insights); and enhanced defect reporting and root cause analysis (compile defect reports with test logs, screenshots and environment data). GUI tests become unstable with UI changes, and GenAI can adapt scripts to dynamic locators and modified interactions; API tests face changing request and response formats, endpoints and authentication, and GenAI can adapt scripts to evolving API specifications and generate diverse test data. GenAI makes mistakes, so check generated output according to the associated risk.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A pull request changes the discount calculation module. The tester gives an LLM the diff, the module-to-test mapping and recent failure history, and asks which regression tests to run first. The LLM selects the checkout and invoice tests touching the changed functions and two flaky UI tests that need self-healing locators. The tester reviews the selection against the mapping before the pipeline runs, because a missed dependency would leave a risky area untested.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Self-healing adapts scripts to minor UI or API changes; it does not decide whether the application behavior is correct. Impact analysis targets regression effort; it does not replace the regression suite. In technique-selection questions, look at the task: precision with checks at each step points to prompt chaining; repetitive output in a fixed pattern points to few-shot; a new or open-ended task where you need help designing the prompt points to meta prompting.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Your team needs 200 keyword-driven test scripts that must all follow the same keyword library and layout. Which technique fits best? Solution: few-shot prompting with examples of correctly structured scripts, because the task is repetitive and has a constrained output format. Add a system prompt describing the keyword library for consistency.

blocks.title: Test monitoring and control; choosing techniques
blocks.text:
Test monitoring needs large and sometimes unstructured data, often already in test management tools. GenAI supports test monitoring and metrics analysis (automating monitoring, analysing trends to predict risks and alert teams about deviations from the plan), test control (insights for reprioritising tests, adjusting schedules and reallocating resources), test completion insights and continuous learning (test completion reports with successes and lessons learned), and enhanced metrics visualisation and reporting (dynamic dashboards and natural-language summaries for all stakeholders).

Choosing techniques: prompt chaining is recommended for complex tasks requiring precision with human verification at each step (test analysis, test design, test automation where each step is checked). Few-shot prompting is recommended for repetitive tasks or tasks with a specific or constrained output format (Gherkin scenarios, keyword-driven tests, reports in a fixed format). Meta prompting is recommended for flexible, dynamic tasks and for crafting prompts for new tasks, using a general description of the objective (complex tasks such as test report analysis and anomaly detection). Techniques can be combined: meta prompting to create an initial prompt, few-shot examples to refine it, and prompt chaining to validate intermediate steps.

blocks.title: Worked case: a sprint status summary
blocks.text: A test manager exports execution results, defect data and coverage from the test management tool and gives them to an LLM with a structured prompt: role (test manager assistant), context (sprint 14 goals and exit criteria), instruction (compute progress against plan, identify trends and risks, propose control actions), constraints (use only the exported data; flag missing data), output format (a short dashboard table and a five-sentence summary for business stakeholders). The manager checks the numbers against the tool before sharing, then uses the suggested reprioritisation as input to test control decisions.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Choose a technique (or combination) for each: (1) you have never analysed performance-test logs with an LLM and are unsure how to phrase the request; (2) monthly test summary reports must follow the company template exactly; (3) deriving test cases from a complex insurance rule where each derived step must be checked before continuing.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Meta prompting: describe the objective and let the LLM help create the prompt, then evaluate and refine it. (2) Few-shot prompting with one or more example reports in the required template. (3) Prompt chaining with human verification at each step. A combination is also valid, for example a meta prompt to draft the initial prompt and a chain to validate steps.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-2.2.3a, HO-2.2.3b, HO-2.2.4, HO-2.2.5)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Document a small keyword library and use few-shot prompting to generate and debug keyword-driven scripts, using a system prompt for a script-checking assistant. Analyse a regression report with a structured prompt chain: compare results with the specification, cluster similar failures, update a known-anomalies list and cross-check findings. Ask an LLM to compute progress and defect-trend metrics from exported test data. For several test tasks, decide which prompting technique fits and justify the choice.

blocks.text:
Automated regression testing (2.2.3): keyword-driven script implementation; impact analysis and test optimisation; self-healing and adaptive tests; automated test reporting and insights; enhanced defect reporting and root cause analysis. Applies to functional and non-functional regression tests; GUI (dynamic locators, modified interactions) and API (changing formats, endpoints, authentication; diverse test data). Check output according to risk.
Test monitoring and control (2.2.4): monitoring and metrics analysis (trends, predicted risks, alerts on deviations), test control (reprioritise, adjust schedules, reallocate resources), test completion insights and continuous learning, metrics visualisation and natural-language reporting.
Choosing techniques (2.2.5): prompt chaining → complex tasks requiring precision and human verification at each step; few-shot → repetitive or constrained-format tasks (Gherkin, keyword-driven, fixed-format reports); meta prompting → flexible, dynamic tasks and new prompts (test report analysis, anomaly detection). Combinations are possible.

lessons.title: 2.3 · Evaluating GenAI results and refining prompts
lessons.summary: Understand the metrics for evaluating GenAI results on test tasks and give examples of techniques for evaluating and refining prompts.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Clear metrics are needed to assess the quality, relevance and effectiveness of GenAI output and to optimise prompting. General metrics: accuracy (overall correctness against expert-written test cases, requirements or other standards, for example how far generated tests cover all specified requirements); precision (correctness with respect to a specific objective, for example how far generated test cases correctly identify anomalies); recall (ability to identify all relevant instances, for example how far generated test cases cover the valid and invalid equivalence partitions of a data class); relevance and contextual fit (whether output is applicable and appropriate, consistent with the test basis and domain requirements); diversity (a wide range of inputs and scenarios, avoiding repetition, covering varied user behaviors and edge cases); execution success rate (the proportion of generated test artefacts that run successfully as is in the test environment, for example scripts without syntax errors or output-format issues); and time efficiency (time saved compared with manual effort). Task-specific metrics can be added. Metrics can be evaluated by manual review or automated comparison with a predefined reference, and because GenAI is non-deterministic, they must be based on statistically relevant data.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: An LLM generated 50 automated API test scripts. 44 ran without syntax or format errors: execution success rate 88%. Of the 12 equivalence partitions defined for the 'amount' field, the generated tests exercised 9: recall 75% for that data class. Writing the scripts took 40 minutes instead of an estimated 6 hours: a time-efficiency gain. A tester reviews whether the tests match the API specification and the payment domain: relevance and contextual fit.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Execution success rate is about whether artefacts run as is, not whether they find defects. Diversity is about variety of scenarios and edge cases, not the number of tests. Because outputs vary between runs, a single run is not enough evidence for a metric: use statistically relevant data.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which metric answers 'Do the generated test cases repeat the same happy path with minor changes?' Solution: diversity. Which answers 'Are the generated tests consistent with our test basis and domain rules?' Relevance and contextual fit.

blocks.title: Evaluating and refining prompts
blocks.text: Techniques to improve results: iterative prompt modification (start with a base prompt and modify it based on actual results, adding context or adjusting wording and terminology); A/B testing of prompts (create several prompt versions and compare their results using predefined metrics to find the most accurate and relevant phrasing or structure); output analysis (examine output for inaccuracies or inconsistencies, for example against the test basis, and refine prompts to avoid similar defects); integrating user feedback (gather testers' views on usefulness, clarity and level of detail and use them to refine prompts); and adjusting prompt length and specificity (sometimes more context helps; sometimes shorter prompts generalise better). Teams can hold prompt evaluation and optimisation sessions and share practices and prompt libraries to standardise techniques, maintain quality and build a culture of learning.

blocks.title: Worked case: A/B testing two prompts
blocks.text: Prompt A asks for 'test cases for the transfer feature'; prompt B adds the role, the acceptance criteria and an output table. Each prompt is run 10 times on the same input. Measured against an expert reference: prompt B achieves higher recall of partitions (on average 11 of 12 versus 7 of 12) and better relevance ratings. Prompt B is adopted and added to the team's prompt library, and the comparison is repeated when the model version changes.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A team finds that generated test cases often use the wrong terminology ('order' instead of 'booking') and are too detailed for their exploratory charters. Name two refinement techniques that address these findings and say how.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Iterative prompt modification: adjust wording and add a terminology constraint or glossary so the model uses 'booking'. Integrating user feedback and adjusting prompt length and specificity: testers report that output is too detailed, so the prompt specifies the desired level of detail or a shorter output format. Output analysis also helps explain where terminology came from.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-2.3.1 and HO-2.3.2)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. For a test case generation task, define a reference set and measure accuracy, recall and execution success rate of the generated output over several runs. Then iterate on a prompt three or four times, using A/B comparison and your own review, recording the metrics for each version.

blocks.text:
Metrics (2.3.1): accuracy, precision, recall, relevance and contextual fit, diversity, execution success rate (artefacts executable as is), time efficiency; plus task-specific metrics. Evaluate by manual review or automated comparison with a predefined reference; base metrics on statistically relevant data because of non-determinism.
Refinement techniques (2.3.2): iterative prompt modification, A/B testing of prompts, output analysis, integrating user feedback, adjusting prompt length and specificity. Prompt evaluation and optimisation sessions; sharing practices and prompt libraries.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Hallucinations, reasoning errors, biases and non-determinism
lessons.summary: Recall the definitions, identify these defects in LLM output (K3), summarise mitigations and recall how to reduce non-determinism.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: LLMs are prone to three kinds of defect that reduce the quality of generated testware. Hallucinations: output that is factually incorrect or irrelevant to the task, such as fictitious or irrelevant test cases, incorrect or non-functioning test scripts, or test cases that verify acceptance criteria that do not exist. Reasoning errors: misinterpreting logical structures such as cause and effect, conditional logic or step-by-step problem solving, leading to wrong conclusions; LLMs rely on pattern matching rather than true logical reasoning, so tasks such as mathematical reasoning, test planning and test case prioritisation are vulnerable. Biases: originate from training data and lead to outputs favouring certain information, approaches or assumptions; for example models trained mainly on English data may underrepresent non-English perspectives, which affects generated test data or refined acceptance criteria. These defects stem from the training data and the inherent limitations of the transformer model. Non-determinism makes them hard to fix: a defect may seem fixed in one output and reappear in another conversation.

blocks.title: Worked example (identifying the defect type)
blocks.text: The project briefing lists three features of an e-shop: cart management, discount codes and order confirmation emails. An LLM proposes four test cases, one of which checks that users can save items to a wishlist. No wishlist is mentioned anywhere: that test case is a hallucination. In a second prompt, the LLM estimates test effort as 3 + 5 + 8 = 15 days for three tasks: a reasoning (arithmetic) error, since the sum is 16. In a third, all generated customer names and addresses are from one country, although the product is sold in twelve: a bias in synthetic test data.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A test case that is plausible in general but has no basis in the provided context is a hallucination, even if the feature might exist in other systems. A wrong conclusion from correct inputs (a miscounted total, a broken dependency order, a wrong condition outcome) is a reasoning error. A systematic skew (for example only functional tests and no non-functional ones, or test data from one population) points to bias.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: An LLM prioritises test cases and places 'delete account' before 'create account', although the dependency was stated in the prompt. What type of defect is this, and how could it be detected? Solution: a reasoning error (dependency logic). Detect it by logical validation in review, and by output testing, for example executing the schedule or checking it automatically against the dependency list.

blocks.title: Detection and mitigation
blocks.text:
Detection, by review or review combined with automated verification. Hallucinations: cross-verification against documentation, requirements and known behavior (tools can cross-reference data sources); domain expertise consultation; and consistency checks between outputs and with known information. Reasoning errors: logical validation of the flow, coherence and structure of the reasoning in review cycles (tools help, complex cases need human judgement); and output testing, such as running generated test cases or scripts against the test objects. Biases: review whether generated testware (test code or synthetic test data) fairly and accurately represents the defined test strategy and coverage requirements, and assess biases by test type, such as underrepresented non-functional tests. The depth of detection depends on the estimated risk for the task.

Mitigation of hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases (more likely with poorly designed prompts or missing context): provide complete context; divide prompts into manageable segments with prompt chaining, verifying each output; use clear, interpretable data formats; select an appropriate model for the task; and compare results across several models. RAG and fine-tuning (chapter 4) are complementary techniques. Mitigation of non-determinism: lower the temperature (narrower probability distribution, more consistent but less creative and more repetitive output) and set random seeds where the implementation allows (same pseudo-random sequence, better reproducibility). Complete reproducibility cannot be guaranteed; automating parts of output verification gives a structured, consistent evaluation.

blocks.title: Worked case: mitigating a planning task
blocks.text: A test manager asks an LLM to estimate effort and prioritise 60 test cases using a long spreadsheet pasted as unformatted text. The result contains arithmetic and dependency errors. Mitigations: give the data as a clear table (interpretable format), include all prioritisation rules and dependencies (complete context), split the task into a chain (estimate, then check, then prioritise, then check), use a reasoning model, compare the result with a second model, and set a low temperature for repeatable output.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: For each output, name the defect type and one detection approach: (1) a generated Selenium script calls a function that does not exist in the framework; (2) generated test data uses only male first names; (3) a decision-table analysis marks a rule as 'discount applies' although its conditions contradict the stated policy; (4) a summary claims 98% of tests passed when the input shows 88%.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Hallucination (non-functioning script); output testing by running the script, or cross-verification against the framework documentation. (2) Bias in synthetic test data; review against the test strategy and coverage requirements. (3) Reasoning error in conditional logic; logical validation in review. (4) Hallucination (factually wrong statement), detectable by cross-verification or consistency checks against the source data.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-3.1.2a and HO-3.1.2b)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Give two different LLMs context that lacks some details and see whether they invent criteria; vary the prompt and observe the effect. Then give an effort-estimation and prioritisation task with complex input to an LLM, an SLM and a reasoning model, compare their results with the exact answer, and try prompt variations to reduce errors.

blocks.text:
Chapter 3 keywords: security, vulnerability, data privacy. GenAI keywords: hallucination, temperature, reasoning error, bias, context manipulation.
Definitions (3.1.1, K1): hallucination (factually incorrect or irrelevant output), reasoning error (misinterpreted logical structures, wrong conclusions; pattern matching rather than logic), bias (from training data; favours certain information, approaches or assumptions). Causes: training data and transformer limitations. Non-determinism makes defects reappear.
Detection (3.1.2, K3): hallucinations → cross-verification, domain expertise consultation, consistency checks; reasoning errors → logical validation, output testing; biases → review against test strategy and coverage, assess test-type biases (e.g., missing non-functional tests). Depth depends on risk.
Mitigation (3.1.3, K2): complete context, divide prompts (prompt chaining with verification), clear data formats, appropriate model, compare across models; RAG and fine-tuning complement. Non-determinism (3.1.4, K1): lower temperature, set random seeds; no full reproducibility; automate some verification.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Data privacy and security risks
lessons.summary: Explain privacy and security risks of using GenAI in testing, give examples of attack vectors and summarise mitigation strategies.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: GenAI can process large amounts of data that may include sensitive or personally identifiable information. Data privacy concerns: unintentional data exposure (outputs accidentally reveal sensitive information); lack of control over data usage (tools may store and process sensitive data without explicit consent or control, risking misuse or unauthorised access); and compliance risks (using GenAI without complying with regulations such as the GDPR could lead to legal disputes). Security risks: LLM-powered test infrastructure can suffer data breaches or unauthorised access; malicious actors can exploit LLM vulnerabilities, such as manipulative attacks, to alter behavior or extract sensitive information; and attackers can introduce malicious input data to mislead LLMs and compromise accuracy or security.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester pastes production customer records into a public chatbot to generate similar test data. Risks: the records may be stored or used by the provider without control (lack of control over data usage), they may surface later in other outputs (unintentional data exposure), and the organisation may be breaching data protection rules (compliance risk). A safer approach: anonymise or pseudonymise first, minimise the data, and use an approved, secure environment.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Know the four attack vectors in the syllabus table and their examples. Context manipulation: requests designed to extract confidential training data, for example exceeding the context window with very long prompts so the model reveals random snippets of training data. Request manipulation: data that disrupts the output, such as an image that lures the model into a different context and provokes hallucinated acceptance criteria. Data poisoning: manipulating training data, such as fake evaluations when rating an AI-generated test report. Malicious code generation: manipulating an LLM into generating backdoors, such as code that opens a channel to a malicious IP address.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Classify: (1) testers who dislike a tool submit deliberately false ratings of its generated test reports, which are used to retrain it; (2) a generated helper script for test setup contains a call that sends data to an unknown external address. Solution: (1) data poisoning; (2) malicious code generation (a backdoor).

blocks.title: Mitigation strategies
blocks.text: Data protection regulations such as the GDPR do not explicitly restrict GenAI, but their safeguards on lawfulness and purpose limitation of collection, processing and storage may limit what can be done. Data privacy measures: data minimisation (avoid processing sensitive data unless legally permitted and use only the necessary amount of non-sensitive data); data anonymisation and pseudonymisation (mask or replace sensitive information with non-identifiable data); secure data storage and transmission (strong encryption and access controls); and resources training (training programs and policies for responsible, ethical use). Additional strategies: systematic human review of generated output; evaluation by comparison with another LLM; choosing a secure operational environment (a commercial secure offering from an LLM provider, an LLM in a secure cloud, or an LLM installed on the organisation's infrastructure, depending on confidentiality); regular security audits and vulnerability assessments; and staying up to date with security best practices. Strategies are complementary and usually combined; involving senior security engineers, legal counsel, the CTO or CISO is highly recommended.

blocks.title: Worked case: choosing an environment
blocks.text: A medical-device company wants GenAI support for test analysis of documents that are highly confidential. A free public chatbot is unsuitable. Options, by increasing control: a commercial secure enterprise offering with contractual data assurances, an LLM in a secure cloud, or an LLM installed on its own infrastructure. Given the confidentiality and regulation, the company chooses an in-house deployment, adds access controls and encryption, pseudonymises patient references in test data, trains its testers and schedules regular security audits, with the CISO and legal counsel involved.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Match each mitigation to a risk: data minimisation; pseudonymisation; secure environment choice; systematic review of generated output; regular security audits. Risks: (1) generated scripts may contain backdoors; (2) a vendor may retain uploaded test data; (3) test data copied from production contains customer names; (4) unknown weaknesses in the LLM-powered test tool; (5) testers paste whole databases when a few fields would do.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Systematic review of generated output (and security audits). (2) Secure environment choice (commercial secure offering, secure cloud or in-house LLM). (3) Pseudonymisation or anonymisation. (4) Regular security audits and vulnerability assessments. (5) Data minimisation.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-3.2.3)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Take a case study of a team using GenAI for testing and list the privacy and security threats you can see (data shared, where it is processed, who can access outputs, what generated code does), then propose mitigations for each.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Privacy concerns (3.2.1): unintentional data exposure; lack of control over data usage; compliance risks (GDPR). Security risks: attacks on LLM-powered test infrastructure (breaches, unauthorised access); exploitation of LLM vulnerabilities (manipulative attacks); malicious input data.
Attack vectors (3.2.2): context manipulation (extract confidential training data, e.g., exceeding the context window), request manipulation (disruptive inputs, e.g., misleading images provoking hallucinations), data poisoning (manipulated training data, e.g., fake ratings), malicious code generation (backdoors, e.g., channel to a malicious IP).
Mitigations (3.2.3): data minimisation, anonymisation and pseudonymisation, secure storage and transmission, resources training; systematic review of output, comparison with another LLM, secure operational environment (commercial secure offering, secure cloud, in-house), regular audits and vulnerability assessments, current security best practices; combine strategies; involve security engineers, legal counsel, CTO or CISO.

lessons.title: 3.3 · Energy consumption and environmental impact
lessons.summary: Explain how task characteristics and model usage affect the energy use and CO2 emissions of GenAI in testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Training and running LLMs uses a large number of specialised computing resources. Because LLMs are offered as web services, their use loads devices, networks and data centres, increasing energy consumption. Energy use rises sharply with usage, and it depends on task complexity and the computational resources required: generating a single image with a powerful model can use about as much energy as fully charging a smartphone, while generating text uses a small percentage of a charge. Accurate data is hard to obtain, but the cumulative effect of millions of users produces significant CO2 emissions, even when a single request seems negligible. Best practices such as limiting unnecessary model interactions are critical to mitigating the environmental risk.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A team runs a nightly job that asks a large multimodal model to describe every one of 3,000 UI screenshots, although only screens changed by the day's commits need checking. Limiting the job to changed screens (about 150) and using a smaller text-only model where no image analysis is needed cuts the number and cost of interactions, and therefore energy use and emissions.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: The impact is not determined by the number of testers alone: task type (image versus text generation), model size and capability, and the frequency of interactions all matter. A single request seems negligible; the cumulative effect is what matters.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which uses more energy per request according to the syllabus example: generating a test report paragraph or generating a mock-up image? Solution: generating the image, which can use about as much energy as fully charging a smartphone, while text generation uses a small percentage of a charge.

blocks.title: Applying the idea in testing
blocks.text: Factors you can influence: choose right-sized models for each test task (an SLM or smaller model for simple classification or formatting tasks), avoid unnecessary or repeated interactions (cache stable answers, batch requests, avoid re-generating unchanged artefacts), prefer text over image generation where both would serve, and keep prompts and context focused so that fewer tokens are processed. These choices also lower recurring costs (section 5.1.3) and match the environmental considerations listed among essential tester skills (section 5.2.1).

blocks.title: Worked case: comparing two approaches
blocks.text: Approach A regenerates the full regression suite with a large reasoning model after every commit (about 40 runs a day). Approach B uses impact analysis to regenerate only affected test scripts with an instruction-tuned model and runs a reasoning model once a day for prioritisation. Approach B has far fewer and lighter interactions, so its energy consumption and CO2 emissions are lower, provided its outputs still meet the team's quality metrics.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: List three changes that would reduce the energy use of a team that asks a chatbot to re-summarise the whole test log every hour, uses the largest available multimodal model for all tasks, and regenerates the same test data each run.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Summarise only new log entries or at meaningful intervals (limit unnecessary interactions); choose a smaller or text-only model for text tasks (right-sized model); store and reuse generated test data instead of regenerating it (avoid repeated generation).

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-3.3.1)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Use an online simulator of GenAI energy use and CO2 emissions to compare several test tasks (text summary, script generation, image analysis) with different model sizes and frequencies, and note which factors change the result most.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text: Energy (3.3.1): training and inference use many specialised resources; web-service use loads devices, networks and data centres; energy rises sharply with usage; depends on task complexity and computational resources (image generation ≈ full smartphone charge, text ≈ a small percentage); accurate data is hard to obtain; cumulative effect of millions of users → significant CO2; mitigate by limiting unnecessary model interactions.

lessons.title: 3.4 · AI regulations, standards and frameworks
lessons.summary: Recall regulations, standards and frameworks relevant to using GenAI in software testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: GenAI's risks in testing (reasoning errors, data privacy, vulnerabilities, environmental impact) should be addressed with general AI regulations, standards and best-practice frameworks. The syllabus lists four. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (standard: AI management system) specifies requirements for managing AI systems within an organisation, promoting recommended practices, consistency and reliability for GenAI in testing. ISO/IEC 23053:2022 (standard: framework for AI systems using machine learning) provides a framework for AI lifecycle processes with emphasis on safety and transparency, and supports data quality, transparency and safety when using GenAI for testing. The EU AI Act (regulation) establishes a legal framework classifying AI applications by risk level and mandates compliance with transparency, accountability and bias mitigation for GenAI used in testing. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (US framework) offers guidelines for managing AI risks with a focus on fairness, transparency and security, supporting fairness and preventing biased test results. Regulations, standards, national laws and frameworks keep evolving, so test organisations must stay up to date.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A European bank introduces GenAI for test design. Its compliance team asks three questions: which AI management system practices apply (ISO/IEC 42001), which legal obligations apply by risk level (EU AI Act), and how the ML lifecycle supports transparency and data quality (ISO/IEC 23053). Its US subsidiary also uses the NIST AI RMF to manage fairness and security risks.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Know the type of each item: ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 23053 are standards, the EU AI Act is a regulation, and the NIST AI RMF is a (US) framework. ISO/IEC 42001 is about the AI management system of an organisation; ISO/IEC 23053 is about a framework for AI systems that use machine learning.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which item establishes a legal framework classifying AI applications by risk level? Solution: the EU AI Act. Which specifies requirements for managing AI systems within an organisation? ISO/IEC 42001:2023.

blocks.title: Using the guidance
blocks.text: In practice, the guidance shapes a test organisation's GenAI strategy (section 5.1.2): process guidelines on sensitive data, transparency obligations such as marking what was generated with GenAI, and quality gates with review of generated testware. It also links to data protection regulation such as the GDPR (section 3.2.3) and to the compliance risks of shadow AI (section 5.1.1).

blocks.title: Worked case: transparency obligations
blocks.text: A team decides that each generated test case carries a 'generated with GenAI; reviewed by <name>' tag, that sensitive data must not leave the approved environment, and that generated scripts pass a review gate. These rules implement transparency, accountability and quality expectations from the regulations and frameworks the organisation follows.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Name the item: (1) a US framework focused on fairness, transparency and security; (2) a standard providing a framework for AI lifecycle processes using machine learning; (3) a standard specifying requirements for an AI management system; (4) a regulation classifying AI by risk.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) NIST AI Risk Management Framework. (2) ISO/IEC 23053:2022. (3) ISO/IEC 42001:2023. (4) EU AI Act.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (standard, AI management system; consistency and reliability). ISO/IEC 23053:2022 (standard, framework for AI systems using ML; lifecycle, safety, transparency, data quality). EU AI Act (regulation; risk-level classification; transparency, accountability, bias mitigation). NIST AI RMF 1.0 (US framework; fairness, transparency, security; prevents biased test results). Keep up to date with evolving regulations, standards, national laws and frameworks.

lessons.title: 4.1 · LLM-powered test infrastructure, RAG and agents
lessons.summary: Explain the architecture of LLM-powered test infrastructure, summarise RAG and explain LLM-powered agents in test automation.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: An LLM-powered test infrastructure integrates an LLM into the test process to enhance automation, reasoning and decision-making. Unlike a traditional chatbot focused on conversation, an LLM-powered test tool processes test-related queries, analyses requirements, generates test cases and evaluates outputs. Its architecture has a front end (the user interface for queries or commands), a back end (processes user input and manages authentication, data retrieval, prompt preparation and interaction with the LLM), external data sources and the LLM itself (a third-party service accessed by API or a custom in-house model) that generates responses from structured prompts. It goes beyond client-server: the LLM is a smart processing component that interprets and reasons about testware; insights are generated dynamically from context such as requirements, code or test results, unlike rule-based chatbots with scripted answers; the back end integrates multiple data sources, such as relational databases for structured test data and vector databases for semantic retrieval using embeddings; and the back end post-processes the LLM's raw output so it aligns with the test conditions before it reaches the front end.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester types 'Which test cases cover the password reset story?' in the tool's front end. The back end authenticates the user, retrieves the story and related test cases from the relational database and similar documents from a vector database, builds a structured prompt and calls the LLM. It then post-processes the answer, for example checking that every cited test case ID exists, before displaying it.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: RAG does not change the model's weights; fine-tuning does. In RAG, retrieval is based on semantic similarity between the embedding of the query and the embeddings of document chunks, not on exact keyword matching. Chunks are typically small (for example 256-512 tokens) to keep retrieval focused and fit the context window.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Put the RAG steps in order: retrieve relevant chunks; split documents into chunks and encode them as embeddings stored in a vector database; encode the user query; generate a response with the retrieved chunks as context. Solution: chunk and encode (preprocessing), encode the query, retrieve by semantic similarity, generate.

blocks.title: RAG and LLM-powered agents
blocks.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation enhances LLMs with additional data sources to increase relevance and accuracy. During preprocessing, large documents are split into chunks, cleaned, processed and encoded into embeddings with pre-trained models, and stored in vector databases for similarity-based retrieval. At inference, the user query is encoded, relevant chunks are retrieved by semantic similarity (retrieval) and fed to the LLM, which combines its existing knowledge with the retrieved data to produce a grounded response (generation). In testing, RAG lets LLM-powered test infrastructure use enterprise data sources such as databases, documentation and repositories in real time, so analysis and design align with the latest specifications, requirements and test data.

LLM-powered agents are specialised GenAI applications designed for semi-autonomous or autonomous processing of defined tasks. They rely on LLMs for language understanding and generation, can process instructions, retrieve context and act by invoking predefined functions called tools, which lets them interact with and manipulate external systems. Autonomous agents operate independently with minimal human intervention using predefined rules, reinforcement learning and adaptive feedback loops; semi-autonomous agents work with periodic human oversight. Multi-agent architectures have several specialised agents that communicate and coordinate ('orchestration') to solve complex problems. In modern tools, agents are often exposed through AI assistants that automate activities across the test lifecycle (analysis, design, implementation, execution and reporting) semi-autonomously, shifting automation from script-based execution to goal-driven, agent-based automation. Agents suffer from the same hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases as LLMs; mitigate with automated verification of their results or by using semi-autonomous agents for critical tasks.

blocks.title: Worked case: an agent for flaky tests
blocks.text: A team deploys a semi-autonomous agent that, each morning, reads the CI results, calls a tool to re-run failed tests, calls another tool to fetch logs, classifies failures as product defects or flaky tests and drafts defect reports. A tester approves each defect report before it is filed. Because the agent can misclassify (reasoning errors) or invent details (hallucinations), its classifications are verified automatically against re-run results and the human approval step remains for critical actions.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A RAG-based assistant answers questions about test procedures from 2,000 internal documents. Answers sometimes cite an outdated procedure. Name two places in the RAG process to investigate and explain why.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Preprocessing: outdated documents may still be chunked and stored in the vector database, so they can be retrieved; refresh or remove them. Retrieval: the semantic similarity search may rank the outdated chunk higher than the current one; check the chunking, embeddings and retrieval settings. Generation can also mix retrieved data with the model's prior knowledge, so verify answers against the source documents.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercises (HO-4.1.2 and HO-4.1.3)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Ask a question about your own test procedures to an LLM with and without RAG over a small set of documents, compare the answers and note strengths and limits. Watch a demonstration, or try a tool, in which an LLM-powered agent automates a repetitive test task, and note which tools it calls and where a human should check its work.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Chapter 4 keywords: test infrastructure. GenAI keywords: fine-tuning, LLM-powered agent, Large Language Model Operations, retrieval-augmented generation, vector database.
Architecture (4.1.1): front end, back end (authentication, data retrieval, prompt preparation, LLM interaction), external data sources, LLM (third-party via API or in-house). Beyond client-server: LLM reasons about testware; dynamic insights from context; multiple sources (relational and vector databases); post-processing of raw output.
RAG (4.1.2): preprocessing (chunks of e.g. 256-512 tokens, embeddings, vector database), retrieval by semantic similarity, generation with retrieved context; access to enterprise data in real time.
Agents (4.1.3): semi-autonomous or autonomous; tools (predefined functions); autonomous (minimal human intervention; rules, reinforcement learning, feedback loops) vs semi-autonomous (periodic oversight); multi-agent orchestration; AI assistants across the test lifecycle; goal-driven agent-based automation; same risks as LLMs; mitigate with automated verification or semi-autonomous agents for critical tasks.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Fine-tuning and LLMOps
lessons.summary: Explain fine-tuning of language models for test tasks and the role of LLMOps in deploying and managing LLMs for testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained language model, an LLM or a small language model (SLM), to specific tasks or domains by further training it on a targeted dataset, so that it learns domain-specific knowledge and nuances and performs better for the intended use. It suits equipping generic LLMs with specialised reasoning for a domain or with a field's vocabulary. SLMs are less resource-intensive, and fine-tuning an SLM can reach high performance for specific tasks without the computational overhead of LLMs. Example: training a model on an organisation's user stories and corresponding test cases so that it generates test cases in the organisation's format and terminology. Challenges: high-quality, task-specific training data to avoid biased or inaccurate results; mitigating overfitting (too specialised to the training data, poor on new data); opacity of the model's reasoning, which complicates debugging and validation; and significant computational resources (for LLMs).

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: An insurer fine-tunes an SLM on 8,000 pairs of its own user stories and approved test cases. The fine-tuned model writes test cases using the insurer's template and terms. Testing shows excellent results on stories similar to the training data but poor results on a new product line: a sign of overfitting. The team adds more varied training examples and keeps human review of generated test cases.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Fine-tuning changes the model by further training; RAG adds retrieved context at inference without changing it. Fine-tuning does not remove the need to review outputs: opacity and possible overfitting remain. LLMOps covers operating LLMs (development, deployment, maintenance); it is not a prompting technique.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Why might a team fine-tune an SLM rather than an LLM for classifying defect reports? Solution: SLMs are less resource-intensive, and a fine-tuned SLM can achieve high performance on a specific task without the computational overhead of an LLM.

blocks.title: LLMOps
blocks.text: LLMOps (Large Language Model Operations) is the set of practices, tools and processes that streamline development, deployment and maintenance of LLMs in production. The way GenAI is used influences LLMOps decisions. Using an AI chatbot: manage data privacy and security risks while optimising cost; use LLM-as-a-Service if assurances are adequate, or in-house infrastructure with open-source licensed LLMs for more control; rigorously assess vendor assurances or internal capabilities. Using a test tool with GenAI capabilities: similar considerations, plus evaluating the tool provider's data security and performance assurances; such tools complement existing processes and need a cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment. In-house development of a GenAI-based test tool: full control of privacy and security risks and careful planning of AI resources (compute, storage, staff training), structured processes for validating and maintaining GenAI-specific developments, and expertise in implementing and deploying LLM-powered test infrastructure. The approaches are not mutually exclusive, and can incorporate RAG and fine-tuning.

blocks.title: Worked case: three approaches at once
blocks.text: A software company uses an approved enterprise chatbot for ad-hoc test ideas, a commercial test management tool with built-in GenAI for test case suggestions, and an in-house agent that triages CI failures. LLMOps decisions differ: for the chatbot, vendor privacy assurances and cost; for the tool, the provider's security and performance assurances and a cost-benefit analysis; for the in-house agent, compute planning, validation and maintenance processes, monitoring and staff skills.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Your organisation forbids sending source code outside its network. Which GenAI usage approach and LLMOps considerations fit a plan to generate unit-test suggestions from code?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: In-house development (or an in-house deployed open-source licensed model behind a chatbot or tool), because it gives full control over data privacy and security. Consider computational resources, data storage, staff training, structured validation and maintenance processes, and the expertise needed to deploy LLM-powered test infrastructure; RAG over the code base or fine-tuning can improve results.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-4.2.1)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. Follow or watch a fine-tuning walkthrough: select an LLM or SLM, prepare a dataset of examples for one test task, fine-tune with an ML framework, then compare outputs of the base and fine-tuned models, paying particular attention to the quality of training data.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Fine-tuning (4.2.1): further training of a pre-trained LLM or SLM on a targeted dataset; domain knowledge, specialised reasoning, vocabulary; SLMs need fewer resources; example: organisation's user stories and test cases. Challenges: high-quality task-specific data, overfitting, opacity, computational resources.
LLMOps (4.2.2): practices, tools and processes for development, deployment and maintenance of LLMs in production. Approaches: AI chatbot (privacy, security, cost; LLM-as-a-Service or in-house open-source), test tool with GenAI (plus provider assurances, cost-benefit analysis, risk assessment), in-house development (full control, resource planning, validation and maintenance processes, expertise). Approaches can coexist and add RAG or fine-tuning.
