lessons.title: 5.1 · Adoption roadmap: shadow AI, strategy, model selection and phases
lessons.summary: Recall the risks of shadow AI, explain a GenAI test strategy, summarise model selection criteria and recall the adoption phases.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Shadow AI is the use of GenAI tools or systems within an organisation without formal approval or oversight. Its risks: information security and data privacy weaknesses (personal AI tools may lack robust security, leading to breaches); compliance and regulatory issues (unapproved tools may breach standards and regulations, with legal consequences); and vague intellectual property (unclear licensing can lead to IP disputes, especially if copyrighted data is processed without authorisation). A strategy and steps for integrating and deploying GenAI help avoid shadow AI. A GenAI test strategy should consider the test objectives to achieve, LLM selection, issues with the input data used for prompting, and compliance with AI standards and regulations; it is the basis for a roadmap and for monitoring progress.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Testers at a retailer use their personal accounts on a free chatbot to analyse defect logs containing customer emails. Nobody approved the tool. Risks: customer data may be stored by the provider (security and privacy weakness), the company may breach data protection rules (compliance), and the licence terms for generated content are unclear (vague intellectual property). The test manager raises the need for an approved tool, usage rules and training as part of a GenAI strategy.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: The adoption phases are discovery, initiation and usage definition, then utilisation and iteration. Discovery is about awareness and capability building, not about full integration. Phases can run in parallel for different use cases, for example test report analysis further along than test automation.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: In which phase does an organisation identify and prioritise practical GenAI use cases and evaluate LLM-powered test infrastructure? Solution: initiation and usage definition. In which phase does it train teams, give access to LLMs and experiment with first use cases? Discovery.

blocks.title: Strategy, model selection and phases
blocks.text:
Key aspects of a GenAI strategy in testing: measurable test objectives for GenAI (increase test productivity, shorten test cycles, improve test quality); selecting LLMs aligned with those objectives, compatible with existing test infrastructure and meeting scalability needs; data quality (accurate, relevant input data protected by robust security procedures); comprehensive training programs for technical and ethical skills; metrics to measure the effectiveness of GenAI results (section 2.3.1); and process guidelines for compliance and ethics, including rules for sensitive data, transparency obligations (what was generated with GenAI) and quality gates with review of generated testware.

Selecting LLMs/SLMs: models differ in functional capabilities (multimodal input, reasoning), technical features (context window size) and licence type (commercial or open source). Benchmarks exist for NLP, code generation or image analysis, but few target test tasks, so criteria are: model performance on the targeted test tasks against the organisation's own benchmarks (using metrics such as those in 2.3.1); fine-tuning potential with domain-specific data; recurring cost (licensing fees and operational expenses within budget); and community and support (active community and detailed documentation).

Adoption phases: (1) discovery: awareness and capability building, training teams on GenAI concepts, giving access to LLMs/SLMs and experimenting with initial use cases to build confidence; (2) initiation and usage definition: identifying and prioritising practical use cases, evaluating LLM-powered test infrastructure, developing expertise and aligning with organisational needs; (3) utilisation and iteration: full integration into test processes with continuous monitoring of progress and tools, measurement and management of the transformation for sustainable benefits and scalability. Address early concerns such as fear of job displacement, which affect adoption and morale.

blocks.title: Worked case: estimating recurring cost
blocks.text: A team plans to analyse 400 regression failures per day. Each analysis sends about 3,000 input tokens and receives 500 output tokens. With a price of 2 currency units per million input tokens and 8 per million output tokens: daily input 1.2 million tokens (2.4 units), daily output 0.2 million tokens (1.6 units), about 4 units per day or about 120 per month, before infrastructure and staff costs. Comparing such estimates for a commercial model and an open-source model hosted in-house is part of the recurring cost criterion.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Name the selection criterion: (1) the model scores 82% recall on the team's own set of 200 reference test cases; (2) the model can be adapted with the company's requirements and test cases; (3) the licence and token prices fit the yearly budget; (4) the model has active forums and detailed documentation.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: (1) Model performance against the organisation's benchmarks. (2) Fine-tuning potential. (3) Recurring cost. (4) Community and support.

blocks.title: Hands-on exercise (HO-5.1.3)
blocks.text: Not examined, but recommended. For one test task, estimate the recurring cost from the number of input and output tokens, the prompts used and the task frequency, using the published pricing of at least one commercial model and the hosting costs of one open-source licensed model, and compare the results.

blocks.text:
Chapter 5 GenAI keyword: shadow AI (use of GenAI tools without formal approval or oversight).
Shadow AI risks (5.1.1, K1): information security and data privacy weaknesses; compliance and regulatory issues; vague intellectual property.
Strategy (5.1.2): measurable test objectives (productivity, shorter cycles, quality); LLM selection aligned with objectives, compatible and scalable; data quality and security; training programs (technical and ethical); effectiveness metrics; process guidelines (sensitive data, transparency obligations, quality gates with review).
Selection criteria (5.1.3): model performance (own benchmarks, metrics from 2.3.1), fine-tuning potential, recurring cost, community and support; models differ in capabilities, technical features, licence types; few benchmarks focus on test tasks.
Phases (5.1.4, K1): discovery; initiation and usage definition; utilisation and iteration. Can run in parallel per use case; address concerns such as fear of job displacement.

lessons.title: 5.2 · Managing change: skills, capabilities and evolving roles
lessons.summary: Explain the skills testers need for GenAI, recall strategies for building team capabilities and recognise how roles and processes shift.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Implementing GenAI needs structured change management: building GenAI skills and evolving traditional roles toward AI-enabled test processes, covering technical and organisational aspects. Essential skills: mastering prompt engineering, understanding model context windows and developing test review methods; combining domain and test expertise with AI skills to evaluate LLM-driven work such as test case generation, defect report analysis and test data generation; assessing LLM capabilities, understanding prompt refinement and evaluating AI-generated testware. Essential knowledge: the inherent risks of GenAI and common mitigations; the data security implications of sharing testware with LLMs; proper data sanitisation (removing or masking sensitive, personal or confidential information) and privacy-preserving prompt engineering; and environmental considerations, such as optimising model selection and usage patterns, right-sizing models and balancing automation benefits with cost and energy consumption.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester prepares to ask an LLM to analyse 300 defect reports. Before sending, they remove customer names and account numbers (data sanitisation), keep the prompt within the context window by batching reports, choose a mid-sized model rather than the largest one (right-sizing) and plan a review of the clustered results against a sample of reports (test review method). Each step reflects an essential skill or knowledge area.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: GenAI does not remove the need for test expertise: testers combine domain and test knowledge with AI skills. Testers move from test design and execution specialists to AI-assisted test specialists who guide and verify AI-generated testware; test managers add AI-based strategy, AI-based risk management and monitoring of AI-based processes.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which activity is a new task for testers in an AI-enabled test organisation: maintaining a test-specific prompt library, or writing the project's business case? Solution: maintaining a test-specific prompt library, together with reviewing AI-based output and refining prompts.

blocks.title: Building capabilities and evolving roles
blocks.text:
Building GenAI capabilities needs a hands-on approach: practising with various LLMs and SLMs, following structured learning paths and gradually developing know-how by sharing within the organisation. Training focuses on practical skills through guided exercises, peer learning and gradual integration of AI into daily tasks. Team members progress from basic prompt creation to focused techniques such as test-specific prompts; a prompt pattern is a reusable template for crafting prompts that guide GenAI to consistent, reliable outputs. Internal communities of practice support knowledge sharing with regular meetings to highlight successes, discuss challenges and refine best practices, sharing prompt pattern libraries and documenting lessons learned across projects and domains.

Evolving processes: testers evolve from test design and execution specialists to AI-assisted test specialists, combining test techniques with skills to guide and verify AI-generated testware; their tasks expand to reviewing AI output, refining prompts and maintaining test-specific prompt libraries. Test managers' responsibilities expand to developing an AI-based test strategy, AI-based risk management and monitoring and control of AI-based test processes; they balance human and AI capabilities, establish AI governance frameworks for use cases, keep teams competent in traditional testing and AI literacy, and coordinate with GenAI-powered test agents, which needs new skills for managing hybrid teams of people and GenAI tools.

blocks.title: Worked case: a community of practice
blocks.text: A test organisation of 60 testers starts a monthly GenAI community of practice. Each session, one team shows a successful use case, another discusses a failure (for example hallucinated acceptance criteria), and the group updates a shared library of test-specific prompt patterns with notes on when each works. New joiners follow a learning path from basic prompts to these patterns.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Classify each item as a tester change or a test manager change: (1) maintaining prompt libraries; (2) AI-based risk management; (3) reviewing AI-generated test cases; (4) coordinating GenAI-powered test agents alongside human testers; (5) establishing AI governance for use cases.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Tester: (1) and (3). Test manager: (2), (4) and (5).

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Skills and knowledge (5.2.1): prompt engineering, context windows, test review methods; domain and test expertise plus AI skills; assessing LLM capabilities, prompt refinement, evaluating AI-generated testware; GenAI risks and mitigations; data security implications, data sanitisation, privacy-preserving prompt engineering; environmental considerations (model selection, usage patterns, right-sized models, cost and energy balance).
Building capabilities (5.2.2, K1): hands-on practice with various LLMs/SLMs, structured learning paths, sharing know-how; guided exercises, peer learning, gradual integration; basic prompts → test-specific prompts; prompt patterns (reusable templates); communities of practice; prompt pattern libraries and lessons learned.
Evolving processes (5.2.3, K1): testers → AI-assisted test specialists (review AI output, refine prompts, maintain prompt libraries); test managers → AI-based test strategy, AI-based risk management, monitoring and control of AI-based processes, balance human and AI, AI governance, AI literacy, hybrid teams with GenAI agents.

lessons.title: Final revision · Turn evidence into an exam decision
lessons.summary: Review key distinctions, the six K3 skills and timed-exam strategy for CT-GenAI v1.1.

blocks.title: Recall and distinguish
blocks.text: Explain each pair with an example: symbolic AI versus classical ML versus deep learning versus GenAI; token versus embedding; context window versus training data; foundation versus instruction-tuned versus reasoning LLM; multimodal LLM versus vision-language model; AI chatbot versus LLM-powered testing application; constraint versus output format; zero-shot versus one-shot versus few-shot; prompt chaining versus meta prompting; system versus user prompt; accuracy versus precision versus recall versus execution success rate; hallucination versus reasoning error versus bias; temperature versus random seed; context manipulation versus request manipulation versus data poisoning versus malicious code generation; anonymisation versus pseudonymisation; RAG versus fine-tuning; autonomous versus semi-autonomous agent; LLM versus SLM; discovery versus initiation versus utilisation.

blocks.title: K3 checklist
blocks.text: GenAI-2.2.1: provide the test basis and needed inputs (risk likelihood and impact for prioritisation), chain generate-prioritise-check coverage, verify each step. GenAI-2.2.2: structured prompt for test cases, few-shot for fixed formats such as Gherkin, chain for prioritisation with dependencies, privacy-preserving synthetic data. GenAI-2.2.3: keyword-driven scripts with few-shot, impact analysis to target regression tests, self-healing for minor UI or API changes, review by risk. GenAI-2.2.4: give exported test data, ask for progress, trends and risks, propose control actions, check numbers. GenAI-2.2.5: chaining for precision with verification, few-shot for repetition and constrained format, meta for new or open tasks. GenAI-3.1.2: hallucination = unsupported by context; reasoning error = wrong logic or arithmetic; bias = systematic skew; choose the matching detection approach.

blocks.title: Timed strategy
blocks.text: Forty questions in 60 minutes is 1.5 minutes per question on average; spend about three minutes on each of the six K3 questions, which are worth two points each. Read stems for BEST, MOST LIKELY, LEAST and NOT, and for the required selection count. In scenario questions, prefer options that verify generated output and supply the inputs the task needs. Unanswered questions score zero. Answers and explanations appear after you submit the mock or when its timer expires.

blocks.title: Review after a paper
blocks.text: For each mistake, name the objective, explain why your option failed and why the key fits better, re-read the linked lesson and write a new example of your own. Treat correct guesses as mistakes. Use short sessions on weak chapters, remembering that practice can expose questions from unopened papers. A repeated paper is useful revision but cannot give fresh readiness evidence.

blocks.title: Explain a GenAI adoption plan
blocks.text: Pick a real test team. Explain which test tasks GenAI should support first and why; how you would structure prompts and which techniques you would use; how you would evaluate results with metrics; which risks (hallucinations, privacy, security, energy, regulation) apply and how you would mitigate them; whether RAG, fine-tuning or agents are justified; how you would select a model and estimate cost; and how roles and skills would change. If you cannot link two decisions, revisit the relevant lesson.

blocks.title: Map risks to mitigations quickly
blocks.text: Hallucination → complete context, cross-verification, domain experts, consistency checks, RAG. Reasoning error → prompt chaining with verification, reasoning model, logical validation, output testing. Bias → review against strategy and coverage, compare models. Non-determinism → lower temperature, seeds, automated verification. Privacy → minimisation, anonymisation or pseudonymisation, secure storage and transmission, training, secure environment. Security → review generated code, audits and vulnerability assessments, best practices. Shadow AI → strategy, approved tools, guidelines. Energy → right-sized models, fewer unnecessary interactions.

questions.prompt: Which type of AI uses a rule-based system and structured knowledge to model human reasoning and decisions?

options.text: Deep learning
Generative AI
Symbolic AI
Classical machine learning

questions.explanation: Symbolic AI uses rule-based systems that represent knowledge with symbols and logical rules. Classical ML learns from prepared data, deep learning learns features with neural networks, and GenAI creates new content using deep learning. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What is tokenization in the context of large language models?

options.text: Breaking text into smaller units, which can be characters, sub-words or words, so that the model can process them
Converting each word into a fixed numerical ID chosen by the tester so that prompts become shorter and cheaper
Replacing personal data in prompts with random tokens so that sensitive values are never sent to the model provider
Splitting a long conversation into several separate sessions so that the model's memory is reset each time

questions.explanation: Tokenization breaks text into tokens, which can be as small as a character or as large as a sub-word or word, so each token can be processed while keeping context. Masking personal data is anonymisation or pseudonymisation, and splitting sessions is not tokenization. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester asks an LLM to analyse a very long test log and notices that details from the start of the log are ignored. Which concept BEST explains this?

options.text: The system prompt overrides user input, so any log text placed before the instructions is discarded
The temperature setting removes the oldest part of the input to keep the answers creative and diverse
The context window limits how many tokens of preceding text the model can consider when generating its response
The embedding step deletes tokens that appear more than once, so the repeated log lines are lost before processing

questions.explanation: The context window is the amount of preceding text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider; very long inputs can exceed it. Temperature controls randomness, embeddings represent tokens as vectors, and the system prompt does not discard user input. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How are instruction-tuned LLMs derived?

options.text: By adding a retrieval database to a foundation model without changing its learned weights
By reducing the parameters of a reasoning model until it fits on a laptop or phone
By fine-tuning foundation models on datasets that pair prompts with expected responses
By training foundation models from scratch on images and audio instead of text data

questions.explanation: Instruction-tuned LLMs are derived from foundation models and fine-tuned with datasets pairing prompts with expected responses, improving alignment with human instructions. Adding retrieval is RAG, and reducing parameters describes smaller models, not instruction tuning. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester gives a multimodal LLM a screenshot of a checkout page together with the related user story. Which use is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Generating the production database schema from the layout of the fields on the screenshot
Identifying discrepancies between the expected results in the story and the visual elements on the screenshot
Proving that the checkout code has no defects because the screenshot matches the user story
Measuring the page's response time under load by analysing the pixels in the screenshot image

questions.explanation: Multimodal LLMs, especially those with vision-language models, can analyse screenshots and GUI wireframes together with text such as user stories, helping testers find discrepancies between expected results and actual visual elements. They cannot measure performance from an image or prove the absence of defects. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.4 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO examples are key LLM capabilities for test tasks described in the syllabus? Select TWO.

options.text: Summarising test results and classifying anomalies by severity and priority
Guaranteeing that generated test cases detect every defect in the test object
Replacing stakeholder reviews by approving requirements on the stakeholders' behalf
Executing performance tests on production servers without any test environment
Identifying ambiguities and missing information in requirements and suggesting clarifying questions

questions.explanation: Requirements analysis and improvement and test result analysis are among the key LLM capabilities listed, together with test case creation, test oracle and test data generation, test automation support and testware creation. LLMs cannot guarantee defect detection, approve requirements for stakeholders or replace test environments. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 17); GenAI-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST compares AI chatbots with LLM-powered testing applications?

options.text: Chatbots offer conversational interaction with immediate responses, while LLM-powered applications integrate LLMs through APIs to perform well-defined, often automated tasks
Chatbots use small language models, while LLM-powered applications use large language models that cannot be accessed through a conversation
Chatbots need no prompt engineering because they are conversational, while LLM-powered applications need prompts because they are automated
Chatbots integrate LLMs through APIs into test frameworks, while LLM-powered applications offer a conversational interface for exploratory questions alone

questions.explanation: AI chatbots provide a conversational interface for immediate, context-aware responses; LLM-powered testing applications integrate LLM capabilities via APIs for well-defined, often automated tasks with more customisation and scalability. Both need strong prompt engineering, and the model size is not the distinction. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 18); GenAI-1.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A structured prompt for analysing a specification contains the line: 'Present the potential defects in a markdown table with the columns ID, requirement, defect type and severity.' To which prompt component does this line MOST LIKELY belong?

options.text: Instruction
Constraints
Output format
Input data

questions.explanation: The line specifies the expected structure of the response, so it belongs to the output format. An instruction states the task itself, constraints restrict how the instruction is applied to the input data, and input data is the material to work on. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which prompt line is an example of the 'role' component?

options.text: Return the scripts as one code block without any explanatory comments.
You are an experienced test automation engineer working on a web shop.
Use the page-object classes from our framework; do not invent new ones.
Generate test scripts for the three login test cases listed below.

questions.explanation: The role defines the perspective or persona the model should adopt, such as a tester or test automation engineer. The other lines are an instruction, a constraint and an output-format specification. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST differentiates prompt chaining, few-shot prompting and meta prompting?

options.text: Prompt chaining guides the model with several examples, few-shot prompting splits a task into steps, and meta prompting removes the need for any review
Prompt chaining splits a task into checked steps, few-shot prompting guides with examples, and meta prompting uses the LLM to create or refine prompts
Prompt chaining links several LLMs to one database, few-shot prompting limits the response length, and meta prompting sets the model's temperature
Prompt chaining uses the LLM to write its own prompts, few-shot prompting gives no examples, and meta prompting checks each intermediate output

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining breaks a task into intermediate steps whose results are checked before continuing; few-shot prompting provides examples; meta prompting uses the LLM to generate or refine prompts with the tester. The distractors swap or misdescribe the techniques. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 22); GenAI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of a system prompt?

options.text: To change with every interaction so that each answer adapts to the user's latest instructions
To carry the specific question that the chatbot's user wants answered in the current interaction
To define the LLM's behavior, personality and operational parameters for the whole conversation
To display the chatbot's internal rules to users so that they can edit them during the session

questions.explanation: A system prompt acts as a predefined command set that defines the LLM's behavior, personality and operational parameters; it stays constant and sets the rules for the entire conversation. The specific question is the user prompt, which changes with each interaction, and system prompts are usually not visible or editable by users. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 23); GenAI-2.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt:
A team receives new, unreviewed user stories for a ticketing app. They want to use GenAI to (1) find problems in the stories, (2) derive acceptance criteria and (3) confirm that every story aspect is covered. Given these steps:
i. Give the stories to the LLM and ask it to identify ambiguities, inconsistencies and missing information; verify the result
ii. Give the corrected stories to the LLM and ask for acceptance criteria; verify them
iii. Give the stories and the verified criteria to the LLM and ask which aspects of the stories are not covered; verify the result
iv. Give the stories to the LLM and ask in a single prompt for complete, defect-free acceptance criteria
v. Give the stories to the LLM and ask it to execute the acceptance tests against the app
Which sequence applies prompt chaining BEST?

options.text: iv, i, v
ii, iii, v
i, ii, iii
iv, iii

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining breaks the task into steps with verification between them: first detect defects in the test basis, then generate acceptance criteria from the corrected stories, then check coverage. Step iv merges everything into one unchecked prompt, and step v asks the LLM to execute tests, which is not a test analysis task. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); GenAI-2.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team writes all acceptance tests as Gherkin scenarios and wants an LLM to produce scenarios for new user stories in exactly the same style. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A single prompt containing all user stories of the release, so that the model learns the scenario style from their volume
Zero-shot prompting with the instruction 'write tests', relying on the model to choose a suitable format by itself
Meta prompting that asks the model to invent a new Gherkin-like format which the team then adopts for future stories
Few-shot prompting with several examples, each pairing a user story and its test conditions with its Gherkin scenarios

questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting is suited to repetitive tasks with a specific output pattern, such as Gherkin test cases; examples pairing stories, test conditions and scenarios model the expected result. Zero-shot gives no pattern, inventing a new format defeats the goal, and many stories without scenarios do not show the style. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 25); GenAI-2.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team uses a keyword-driven framework with a documented keyword library and wants GenAI to create new regression test scripts. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Meta prompting that asks the model to design a new keyword library, replacing the documented one used by the team
Few-shot prompting with examples of correct scripts that use the library's keywords, then reviewing the generated scripts
Prompting the model to run the existing scripts in production and rewrite those that fail during the next release
Zero-shot prompting that asks for plain Python code, because keywords restrict the model's creativity in regression testing

questions.explanation: LLMs can implement test scripts with keyword-driven frameworks by mapping predefined keywords to test steps; few-shot examples guide the model to the required pattern, and generated scripts must be checked. Dropping the keywords, replacing the library or running scripts in production does not apply GenAI appropriately. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 27); GenAI-2.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A test manager exports execution results, defect data and coverage from the test management tool and wants GenAI support for test monitoring. Which prompt is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Ask the model to estimate progress from its general knowledge of similar projects, without attaching the exported data to the prompt
Ask the model to change the exit criteria so that the current results meet them, and report the sprint as completed to stakeholders
Provide the exported data with the sprint goals and exit criteria, ask for progress against plan, trends and risks, and specify a short dashboard table as output
Ask the model to generate new defect data that fills the gaps in the export, so that the dashboard looks complete for the steering group

questions.explanation: GenAI can analyse test data to produce monitoring metrics, trends and predicted risks; providing the data, context and an output format makes the result accurate and usable. Estimating without data invites hallucination, changing exit criteria is not monitoring, and inventing data is unacceptable. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.4 (p. 28); GenAI-2.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A test team must produce 150 keyword-driven test scripts that all follow the same layout and keyword library. Which prompting technique fits this task BEST?

options.text: Zero-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Prompt chaining
Meta prompting

questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting is recommended for repetitive tasks or tasks with a specific or constrained output format, such as keyword-driven testing, because the examples show the required pattern. Prompt chaining suits complex tasks needing verification at each step, and meta prompting suits new or flexible tasks. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.5 (p. 29); GenAI-2.2.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: An LLM generated 50 automated test scripts, and 44 of them ran in the test environment without syntax or output-format errors. Which metric does this measure?

options.text: Execution success rate
Time efficiency
Relevance and contextual fit
Recall

questions.explanation: Execution success rate measures the proportion of generated test artefacts that can be executed successfully as is in the test environment, here 44 of 50 (88%). Recall concerns finding all relevant instances, diversity concerns variety, and time efficiency concerns time saved. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.1 (p. 31); GenAI-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team creates three versions of a prompt for generating API test cases and compares their outputs against the same predefined metrics. Which refinement technique is this?

options.text: Output analysis
A/B testing of prompts
Integrating user feedback
Iterative prompt modification

questions.explanation: A/B testing of prompts creates multiple versions and evaluates which produces better results based on predefined metrics, showing which phrasing or structure works best. Output analysis examines errors in output, user feedback gathers testers' views, and iterative modification evolves one base prompt. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.2 (p. 32); GenAI-2.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is a hallucination in the output of an LLM?

options.text: Generated content that appears factually incorrect or irrelevant to the given task
A different answer to the same prompt caused by probabilistic sampling
A systematic preference for certain information inherited from training data
A wrong conclusion drawn from correct inputs through faulty logical steps

questions.explanation: Hallucinations occur when an LLM generates output that appears factually incorrect or irrelevant to the task, such as test cases verifying non-existent acceptance criteria. Faulty logic describes reasoning errors, systematic preferences describe bias, and varying answers describe non-determinism. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt:
A library management system's project briefing lists three features: borrowing books, returning books and calculating overdue fines. An LLM proposes these test cases:
A. Verify that a member can borrow up to the permitted number of books
B. Verify that a returned book becomes available to other members
C. Verify that a fine is calculated for each day a book is overdue
D. Verify that a member can rate a book and see the average rating
Which test case MOST LIKELY represents a hallucination?

options.text: A
B
D
C

questions.explanation: Rating books is not mentioned in the briefing, so a test case for it is invented content irrelevant to the given task: a hallucination. Test cases A, B and C trace to the three listed features. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester's prompts for generating test conditions often lack the acceptance criteria and domain rules, and the output contains invented details. Which mitigation addresses this cause MOST directly?

options.text: Providing complete context in the prompt with all the information the task needs
Raising the temperature, so that the model explores more possibilities before generating the conditions
Shortening the prompt to one sentence, so that the model has less text to misinterpret while generating
Asking for the output as an image, so that invented details are easier to spot when reviewing the result

questions.explanation: Hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases are more likely when relevant contextual input is lacking; providing complete context guides the AI to accurate results. Raising temperature increases randomness, a one-sentence prompt removes more context, and image output does not address the cause. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which setting can be lowered during inference to make LLM outputs more consistent?

options.text: Token count
Temperature
Embedding size
Context window

questions.explanation: Lowering the temperature narrows the probability distribution during response generation, reducing randomness and giving more consistent outputs, at the cost of creativity and diversity. The other settings do not control sampling randomness. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.4 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which TWO are data privacy concerns of using GenAI in software testing listed in the syllabus? Select TWO.

options.text: GenAI tools may need a context window that is larger than the test basis provided
GenAI outputs may accidentally reveal sensitive information from earlier inputs or training
GenAI tools may store and process sensitive data without explicit consent or control
GenAI outputs may contain too few tokens to describe a test case in sufficient detail
GenAI tools may refuse to process test data that contains numbers or special characters

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists unintentional data exposure, lack of control over data usage, and compliance risks with regulations such as the GDPR as data privacy concerns. The distractors describe limitations that are not privacy concerns. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which attack vector involves sending requests designed to extract confidential training data from an LLM, for example by overloading it with extremely long prompts?

options.text: Data poisoning
Malicious code generation
Context manipulation
Request manipulation

questions.explanation: Context manipulation sends requests designed to extract confidential training data; overloading the context window with long prompts could make the model reveal random snippets of training data. Request manipulation disrupts output, data poisoning manipulates training data, and malicious code generation creates backdoors. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A helper script that an LLM wrote for test environment setup contains a command that opens a connection to an unknown external IP address. Which attack vector does this MOST LIKELY illustrate?

options.text: Malicious code generation
Data poisoning
Request manipulation
Context manipulation

questions.explanation: Manipulating an LLM to generate backdoors, such as external command calls or code that opens a communication channel to a malicious IP, is malicious code generation. The other vectors target training data or disrupt outputs. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team only needs order totals and dates to test a reporting feature, but testers paste complete customer records into prompts. Which mitigation addresses this MOST directly?

options.text: Data poisoning: add misleading records to the prompts so that real data cannot be identified
Higher temperature: increase randomness so that the model forgets the customer records sooner
Longer prompts: include more records so that each customer's data is less visible in the output
Data minimisation: use only the necessary amount of non-sensitive data in testing with GenAI

questions.explanation: Data minimisation means avoiding the processing of sensitive data unless legally permitted and using only the necessary amount of non-sensitive data. Data poisoning is an attack, temperature does not affect data retention, and more data increases risk. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 39); GenAI-3.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the energy consumption of GenAI tasks is consistent with the syllabus?

options.text: Generating a single image with a powerful model can use about as much energy as fully charging a smartphone, while text generation uses much less
Generating any output uses the same energy, because the model's size is fixed regardless of the task it performs
Generating outputs uses no measurable energy, because LLMs run as web services in data centres far from the user
Generating text uses more energy than generating images, because text requires more tokens than any image ever needs

questions.explanation: The syllabus cites that generating one image with a powerful AI model can consume as much energy as fully charging a smartphone, while generating text consumes only a small percentage of a charge. Energy depends on the task and resources, and web services still consume energy in data centres. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.3.1 (p. 40); GenAI-3.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item establishes a legal framework that classifies AI applications by risk level?

options.text: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
EU AI Act

questions.explanation: The EU AI Act is a regulation establishing a legal framework addressing AI risks and classifying applications by risk level. ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 23053 are standards, and the NIST AI RMF is a US framework. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.4.1 (p. 41); GenAI-3.4.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: In a typical LLM-powered test infrastructure, which component handles authentication, data retrieval, prompt preparation and interaction with the LLM?

options.text: The back end
The front end
The test object
The vector database

questions.explanation: The back end processes user input and manages critical functions such as authentication, data retrieval, prompt preparation and interaction with the LLM. The front end is the user interface, a vector database is one data source, and the test object is what is being tested. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.1 (p. 44); GenAI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, what happens during preprocessing?

options.text: Documents are split into chunks, cleaned and encoded into embeddings that can be stored in a vector database
The documents are translated into prompts, and each prompt is sent once to the LLM to warm up its cache
The LLM is retrained on all of the documents so that its weights contain the latest specifications and test data
The user query is sent to several LLMs, and the most common answer is stored as the reference response

questions.explanation: During preprocessing, large documents are broken into chunks (for example 256-512 tokens), cleaned, processed and encoded into high-dimensional embeddings, which can be stored in vector databases for similarity-based retrieval. RAG does not retrain the model, poll several LLMs or warm a cache. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.2 (p. 45); GenAI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What distinguishes LLM-powered agents from traditional AI chatbots?

options.text: Agents use rule-based scripts instead of an LLM, which makes them fully deterministic and free of hallucinations and biases
Agents can act by invoking predefined functions called tools, which lets them interact with and change external systems
Agents are limited to one prompt per day, while chatbots can process an unlimited number of prompts from many testers
Agents answer questions in a conversation, while chatbots execute test scripts and file defect reports in the tracker

questions.explanation: Unlike traditional chatbots focused on question-response interactions, LLM-powered agents can perform tasks by invoking a predefined set of functions, called tools, allowing them to interact with and manipulate external systems. Agents rely on LLMs and share their risks. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.3 (p. 46); GenAI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does fine-tuning a language model for a test task involve?

options.text: Adding retrieved documents to each prompt at inference time so that the unchanged model can answer domain questions
Further training a pre-trained LLM or SLM on a targeted dataset so that it learns domain-specific knowledge and nuances
Writing a detailed system prompt so that the model behaves like a domain expert without any change to its parameters
Lowering the temperature and setting a random seed so that the model gives the same domain-specific answers at each request

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained language model (LLM or SLM) to specific tasks or domains by further training on a targeted dataset. Adding retrieved documents is RAG, temperature and seeds reduce variability, and a system prompt changes behavior without training. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 47); GenAI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is LLMOps?

options.text: A licensing model under which LLM vendors charge organisations per operation rather than per token used
The practices, tools and processes that streamline the development, deployment and maintenance of LLMs in production
A prompting technique that splits complex test tasks into a chain of smaller prompts with verification steps
A test level at which LLM-generated test cases are executed against the system before acceptance testing

questions.explanation: LLMOps (Large Language Model Operations) refers to the practices, tools and processes for developing, deploying and maintaining LLMs in production environments. Chained prompts are prompt chaining, and LLMOps is neither a test level nor a licensing model. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 48); GenAI-4.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is shadow AI?

options.text: A test approach in which a new model processes live requests without affecting user responses
The use of GenAI tools or systems within an organisation without formal approval or oversight
A backup LLM that runs in parallel with the main model and takes over if the main model fails
A hidden system prompt that defines the behavior of a chatbot without being visible to its users

questions.explanation: Shadow AI is the use of GenAI tools or systems within an organisation without formal approval or oversight. A hidden instruction set is a system prompt, and running a new model in parallel on live requests resembles shadow testing, which is a different concept. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which example is a measurable test objective for a GenAI strategy in testing?

options.text: Use GenAI as much as possible in every test activity, starting immediately and without any further planning
Become an AI-first test organisation with the most innovative prompt library in the entire industry
Shorten the regression test design cycle by 30% within two releases while keeping review findings stable
Ensure that testers feel positive about GenAI tools in general, regardless of the results they obtain

questions.explanation: A GenAI strategy begins with defining measurable test objectives, such as increasing test productivity, shortening test cycles and improving test quality. The distractors are not measurable or not tied to test outcomes. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test manager evaluates two LLMs by running both on 200 reference test cases from the organisation's own projects and comparing the results with predefined metrics. Which selection criterion is being applied?

options.text: Model performance
Recurring cost
Community and support
Fine-tuning potential

questions.explanation: Model performance evaluates the model on the targeted test tasks against the organisation's own benchmarks using metrics such as those in section 2.3.1. Fine-tuning potential, recurring cost and community support are separate criteria. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which list gives the phases of adopting GenAI in a test organisation in the correct order?

options.text: Utilisation and iteration; discovery; initiation and usage definition
Discovery; utilisation and iteration; initiation and usage definition
Discovery; initiation and usage definition; utilisation and iteration
Initiation and usage definition; discovery; utilisation and iteration

questions.explanation: The three phases are discovery (awareness and capability building), initiation and usage definition (identifying and prioritising use cases), and utilisation and iteration (full integration with continuous monitoring). The distractors change the order. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Before sharing defect reports with an LLM, a tester removes customer names and account numbers from them. Which essential knowledge area does this reflect?

options.text: Selecting right-sized models to reduce computational overhead
Fine-tuning of language models on defect data
Context window optimisation for long defect logs
Data sanitisation and privacy-preserving prompt engineering

questions.explanation: Testers should understand the data security implications of sharing testware with LLMs, implement proper data sanitisation (removing or masking sensitive, personal or confidential information) and follow privacy-preserving prompt engineering practices. The other areas do not describe removing sensitive data. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is a prompt pattern, as described in the syllabus?

options.text: A rule that limits the number of prompts per day so that the organisation's recurring cost stays predictable
A reusable template for crafting effective prompts that guide GenAI toward consistent, reliable outputs
A recurring error in LLM outputs that appears whenever the same prompt is submitted more than once in a session
A graphical chart that shows how often each tester submitted prompts during the last month of the project

questions.explanation: A prompt pattern is a reusable template for crafting effective prompts that guide GenAI toward consistent and reliable outputs; prompt pattern libraries are shared within communities of practice. The other options are not definitions from the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: How does the role of testers change in an AI-enabled test organisation, according to the syllabus?

options.text: Testers become data scientists who train new language models instead of designing and executing test cases
Testers become prompt typists who forward requirements to an LLM and file its output without checking it for errors
Testers become observers whose test techniques are replaced entirely by autonomous agents in every project
Testers become AI-assisted test specialists who guide and verify AI-generated testware using their expertise in test techniques

questions.explanation: Testers evolve from test design and execution specialists to AI-assisted test specialists, combining their expertise in test techniques with skills to guide and verify AI-generated testware. The other descriptions remove the tester's verification role or overstate automation. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 53); GenAI-5.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which type of AI is a data-driven approach that requires data preparation, feature selection and model training, and can be used to categorise defects?

options.text: Classical machine learning
Generative AI using pre-trained LLMs
Symbolic AI using logical rules
Vision-language modelling

questions.explanation: Classical machine learning is data-driven and needs data preparation, feature selection and model training; the syllabus mentions defect categorisation and predicting software problems as uses. Symbolic AI relies on explicit rules, and GenAI applies pre-trained models directly. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What are embeddings in large language models?

options.text: Short test examples embedded in a prompt to show the model the expected output for a given input
Hidden instructions embedded in the system prompt that users of the chatbot cannot see or change
Numerical vectors that represent tokens in a high-dimensional space, placing tokens with similar meanings close together
Code snippets embedded in generated test scripts that call the LLM's API during test execution

questions.explanation: Embeddings are numerical representations of tokens that encode semantic, syntactic and contextual relationships as vectors; similar tokens are positioned close together. Examples in a prompt are few-shot prompting, hidden instructions are the system prompt, and API calls in scripts are unrelated. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why can the same prompt produce different test cases when it is submitted to an LLM several times?

options.text: LLMs select a different training dataset for each prompt, depending on the time of day of the request
LLMs retrain their weights after each prompt, so the model changes between two identical submissions
LLMs are non-deterministic because their inference is probabilistic and depends on hyperparameter settings
LLMs store each previous answer and deliberately avoid repeating any test case that they have already produced

questions.explanation: LLMs exhibit non-deterministic behavior primarily because of the probabilistic nature of inference and hyperparameter settings, so identical inputs can give varying outputs. Models do not retrain on each prompt, deliberately avoid repetition or switch training data. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which test task is MOST likely to benefit from a reasoning LLM rather than an instruction-tuned LLM?

options.text: Working out an execution order for 40 test cases that have dependencies, priorities and limited environments
Rewriting a short test summary report in a more formal tone for the steering committee meeting
Translating a set of existing test case titles from English into Spanish for a regional test team
Reformatting a list of defect identifiers into a comma-separated line for a status email

questions.explanation: Reasoning LLMs emphasise logical inference and multi-step problem solving, so they suit high-cognitive-load tasks such as multi-constraint test scheduling. Rewriting, translating and reformatting need little reasoning and suit instruction-tuned models. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: How do multimodal LLMs typically handle image input before processing it in the transformer model?

options.text: Images are stored in a vector database, and the transformer reads the file names returned by the database
Images are converted into alternative text by a human annotator, and that text alone is passed to the transformer
Images are compressed into a single token, and the transformer predicts which training image is most similar
Tokenization is adapted for each data type; for example, images are converted into embeddings by vision-language models

questions.explanation: To handle several modalities, tokenization is adapted for each data type; for example, images are converted into embeddings using vision-language models before the transformer processes them. Human alt text, single-token compression or file names are not the mechanism described. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.4 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester asks an LLM to propose the expected total for an order of three items under a stated discount rule. Which LLM capability is this?

options.text: Test result analysis
Requirements improvement
Testware maintenance
Test oracle generation

questions.explanation: Helping to generate expected results is test oracle generation. Requirements improvement concerns the test basis, test result analysis summarises and classifies results, and testware maintenance keeps documents up to date. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 17); GenAI-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test team needs to generate thousands of synthetic test data records in a fixed format every night within its existing automation framework. Which interaction model fits BEST?

options.text: An AI chatbot conversation in which a tester copies the generated records into the framework manually
A meta prompt typed into a chatbot each evening so that the model can design a new data format daily
An LLM-powered testing application that calls the LLM through an API and is embedded in the framework
An AI chatbot used by stakeholders to explore the data requirements and suggest additional test ideas

questions.explanation: LLM-powered testing applications integrate LLM capabilities via APIs, offering customisation and scalability to automate repetitive tasks such as test data synthesis within existing frameworks. Chatbots suit interactive, exploratory work rather than nightly high-volume generation. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 18); GenAI-1.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which prompt line is an example of a constraint?

options.text: The feature under test lets retail customers set up standing orders in the mobile app.
Use only the customer data provided below and do not invent new account numbers.
You are a senior test analyst responsible for the payments domain of the bank.
Write the test conditions as a numbered list with one condition on each line.

questions.explanation: Constraints outline restrictions or special considerations, specifying how the instruction is applied to the input data, such as using only the provided data. The other lines are a role, context and output format. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which prompt line provides context rather than an instruction?

options.text: Identify missing acceptance criteria for the user story below and suggest wording for each one.
The application is a mobile banking app for retail customers; the feature under test is standing orders.
Derive boundary values for the amount field and list the expected result for each value.
Prioritise the generated test conditions by risk, using the likelihood and impact values given.

questions.explanation: Context gives background information the model needs to determine the test conditions, such as the test object and the functionality under test. The other lines are directives describing tasks, which belong to the instruction component. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A prompt contains exactly one example of a user story with its expected test conditions, followed by a new user story to analyse. Which technique is this?

options.text: Few-shot prompting
One-shot prompting
Meta prompting
Zero-shot prompting

questions.explanation: One-shot prompting provides one example to demonstrate the expected result. Zero-shot uses no example, few-shot uses more than one, and meta prompting asks the LLM to help create the prompt. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 22); GenAI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about user prompts is correct?

options.text: They replace the system prompt after the first interaction, so that all later responses ignore the developer's rules
They set the formal tone, domain rules and forbidden behaviors that apply to every response in the conversation
They are defined once by the developer, stay constant for the session and are hidden from the chatbot's users
They contain the user's actual input, change with each interaction and form the immediate context for each response

questions.explanation: The user prompt represents the actual input or question from the chatbot's user, changes with each interaction, is directly visible and forms the immediate context. The model considers both the system prompt and the current user prompt; the other options describe system prompts or misstate their interplay. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 23); GenAI-2.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester asks an LLM to prioritise 30 test conditions for an online payment feature by risk. Which addition to the prompt is MOST important for a useful result?

options.text: Risk likelihood and impact information for each test condition, with relevant factors such as regulatory and user-facing aspects
A request to invent risk ratings, so that the model can prioritise even when no risk information is available
A higher temperature setting, so that the model proposes more varied priorities for the test conditions it receives
A list of all the team members, so that the model can assign each test condition to a tester by their seniority

questions.explanation: With information on the risk likelihood and impact for each test condition, an LLM can help prioritise test effort, considering aspects such as regulatory compliance, user-facing features and historical defect data. Without it the model would invent priorities; temperature and team lists do not provide risk information. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); GenAI-2.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester needs realistic customer records for testing a loan application without exposing real customers. Which prompt BEST applies GenAI to this test implementation task?

options.text: Ask for synthetic records resembling production distributions, including extreme values, with no real personal data
Paste a sample of real customer records into the prompt and ask the model to copy them with the names changed to fictional ones
Ask the model to download real records from public websites so that the test data is realistic, current and varied
Ask for records with the most common values only, so that the generated test data reflects typical customers precisely

questions.explanation: GenAI can synthesise representative, privacy-preserving test data that resembles production data, covering extreme situations and varied conditions without exposing sensitive information. Pasting real records risks exposure, typical values alone miss edge cases, and scraping public data raises privacy and legal issues. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 25); GenAI-2.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A pull request changes the module that calculates delivery charges. The full regression suite takes eight hours. How can GenAI BEST support regression testing for this change?

options.text: Run the full suite twice in parallel, because GenAI can then compare the two runs to find flaky tests automatically
Skip regression testing for this module, because GenAI can confirm from the diff alone that the change introduced no defects
Regenerate the entire regression suite from scratch, because existing tests become invalid whenever any code changes
Analyse the code change with the module-to-test mapping to identify high-risk areas and select targeted regression tests, then review the selection

questions.explanation: GenAI can perform impact analysis on code changes to identify high-risk areas and enable targeted regression testing; the output still needs review according to the risk. A diff alone cannot prove the absence of defects, and regenerating or duplicating the suite does not target the change. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 27); GenAI-2.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: GenAI analysis shows that critical payment tests are behind schedule while low-risk report tests are complete. How should GenAI output be used for test control?

options.text: As input for reprioritising tests and reallocating resources toward the payment area, with the decision made by the test manager
As an automatic decision to stop all payment testing, because the model has identified that area as the main source of the delay
As a reason to remove the payment tests from the plan, because GenAI predicts that the payment feature contains no defects
As evidence that the exit criteria are met, because the completed report tests compensate for the missing payment tests

questions.explanation: GenAI can assist test control by providing insights for reprioritising tests, adjusting schedules and reallocating resources so that testing stays focused on high-priority areas; the test manager remains responsible for decisions. Stopping critical tests, treating unrelated completed tests as compensation or dropping tests based on a prediction is inappropriate. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.4 (p. 28); GenAI-2.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester must derive test cases from a complex insurance rule. Each intermediate result (conditions, decision rules, test cases) must be checked for correctness before continuing. Which prompting technique fits this task BEST?

options.text: One-shot prompting
Prompt chaining
Meta prompting
Few-shot prompting

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining is recommended for complex tasks requiring precision with human verification at each step, such as test analysis and test design where each step is checked for correctness. Few-shot suits repetitive output patterns, and meta prompting suits crafting prompts for new tasks. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.5 (p. 29); GenAI-2.2.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Generated test cases for a booking feature mostly repeat the same happy path with minor variations and rarely explore edge cases. Which metric would reveal this weakness?

options.text: Time efficiency
Precision
Diversity
Execution success rate

questions.explanation: Diversity evaluates whether a wide range of inputs and scenarios is covered, avoiding repetition and exploring various user behaviors and edge cases. Execution success rate concerns whether artefacts run, precision concerns correctness for a specific objective, and time efficiency concerns time saved. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.1 (p. 31); GenAI-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO are techniques for evaluating and iteratively refining prompts described in the syllabus? Select TWO.

options.text: Raising the temperature until the generated output matches the expected result on the first run
Rejecting each prompt that fails once, because a refined prompt cannot reuse earlier wording
Starting from a base prompt and adjusting its context or wording based on actual results
Gathering testers' feedback on usefulness and level of detail and using it to refine prompts
Removing the role and context components so that the model relies on its own training alone

questions.explanation: Iterative prompt modification and integrating user feedback are listed refinement techniques, along with A/B testing, output analysis and adjusting prompt length and specificity. Raising temperature increases randomness, removing components reduces guidance, and refinement builds on earlier prompts. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.2 (p. 32); GenAI-2.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is a reasoning error in the output of an LLM?

options.text: Output favouring certain approaches or assumptions because of the composition of the model's training data
Output that differs between two identical prompts because inference samples its tokens from a probability distribution
A misinterpretation of logical structures such as cause and effect or conditional logic, leading to wrong conclusions
Output containing invented facts, such as test cases for features that are not mentioned in the test basis

questions.explanation: Reasoning errors occur when LLMs misinterpret logical structures, such as cause-and-effect relationships, conditional logic or step-by-step problem solving, leading to incorrect conclusions. The other options describe hallucinations, bias and non-determinism. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A tester gives an LLM these effort estimates: test design 4 days, test environment setup 3 days, execution 6 days, reporting 2 days. The LLM states: 'The total effort is 14 days, so the work fits the planned three-week window of 15 working days with one day to spare.' What should the tester conclude?

options.text: The output contains a reasoning error: the total is 15 days, so the window has no slack left
The output shows bias: the LLM favoured the larger estimates provided in the prompt
The output contains a hallucination: the LLM invented an estimate for reporting
The output is correct: the planned window still covers the stated total effort

questions.explanation: The sum 4 + 3 + 6 + 2 is 15, not 14, so the conclusion about a spare day is wrong; this is a reasoning (arithmetic) error, detectable by logical validation. No estimate was invented, no systematic skew is visible, and the conclusion does not follow from the inputs. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which mitigation for reasoning errors does the syllabus describe as dividing prompts into manageable segments?

options.text: Using few-shot prompting to add as many examples as possible so that the model copies a correct line of reasoning
Using a higher temperature so that the model generates several different chains of reasoning in a single response
Using prompt chaining to split a complex task into smaller steps and verifying each output before moving on
Using a longer context window so that the whole task fits into one prompt and no intermediate checks are needed

questions.explanation: Splitting complex prompts into smaller steps with prompt chaining, and verifying each output before the next step, helps detect reasoning errors early. More examples, higher temperature or one larger prompt without checks do not provide that segment-by-segment verification. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is a drawback of lowering an LLM's temperature to reduce variability?

options.text: Responses become longer, because the model adds more detail to each answer
Responses become less creative and diverse, and may become repetitive
Responses become slower, because the model checks each token twice
Responses become hallucinated, because the model invents missing facts

questions.explanation: Lowering the temperature reduces randomness but also limits creativity and diversity, making outputs more repetitive or overly deterministic. It does not lengthen responses, double-check tokens or cause hallucinations. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.4 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: A tester pastes production customer records into an unapproved public chatbot to generate similar test data. Which risk does the syllabus describe as a compliance risk in this situation?

options.text: Using GenAI tools without complying with data protection regulations such as the GDPR, which could lead to legal disputes
Receiving test data in a format that does not match the import tool, which could delay test execution by several days
Receiving fewer test records than requested, because the chatbot limits the number of records it generates per prompt
Paying more than planned for test data, because public chatbots charge per generated record rather than per token that is used

questions.explanation: Compliance risk means using GenAI tools without complying with data protection regulations such as the GDPR, which could lead to legal disputes. Format, quantity and pricing problems are not the privacy or compliance concerns described. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester uploads a wireframe that contains hidden visual elements. The LLM then generates acceptance criteria for an unrelated product. Which attack vector does this illustrate?

options.text: Data poisoning
Context manipulation
Request manipulation
Malicious code generation

questions.explanation: Request manipulation introduces data that disrupts the AI's output, for example images that lure the AI into a different context and provoke hallucinations about acceptance criteria. Context manipulation targets confidential training data, data poisoning manipulates training data, and malicious code generation creates backdoors. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does data poisoning mean as an attack vector in GenAI test processes and tools?

options.text: Manipulating the data used to train or improve the model, such as providing fake evaluations of AI-generated test reports
Uploading misleading images that lure the model into another context so that it hallucinates acceptance criteria
Manipulating the model to generate backdoors, such as external command calls, in the scripts that it produces
Sending very long prompts that overload the context window so that the model reveals parts of its training data

questions.explanation: Data poisoning manipulates training data, with the syllabus example of providing fake evaluations when rating the results of an AI-generated test report. The other options describe context manipulation, request manipulation and malicious code generation. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which mitigation replaces sensitive information in test data with non-identifiable data before it is used in prompts?

options.text: Data anonymisation and pseudonymisation
Comparison of outputs with another LLM
Secure data storage and transmission
Regular security audits and vulnerability assessments

questions.explanation: Anonymisation and pseudonymisation mask or replace sensitive information with non-identifiable data. Secure storage and transmission use encryption and access controls, audits find weaknesses, and comparing LLMs evaluates outputs. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 39); GenAI-3.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why should a test organisation care about the energy use of individual GenAI requests that each seem negligible?

options.text: Because energy use is billed to the tester personally, so each request directly reduces the individual tester's monthly salary
Because the cumulative effect across many users and interactions results in substantial energy use and CO2 emissions
Because each individual request uses more energy than a typical data centre consumes in a day of normal operation
Because regulations forbid GenAI requests that use energy, so each request must be approved by an energy auditor

questions.explanation: While a single search or text generation may seem negligible, the cumulative effect across millions of users results in substantial environmental strain and significant CO2 emissions. The other claims are not in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.3.1 (p. 40); GenAI-3.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which standard specifies requirements for managing AI systems within an organisation?

options.text: EU AI Act
NIST AI Risk Management Framework

questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (AI management system) specifies requirements for managing AI systems within an organisation. ISO/IEC 23053 provides a framework for AI systems using machine learning, the EU AI Act is a regulation and the NIST AI RMF is a risk management framework. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.4.1 (p. 41); GenAI-3.4.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: How does an LLM-powered test infrastructure go beyond a traditional client-server model?

options.text: The LLM acts as a smart processing component that interprets and reasons about testware, generating insights dynamically from context
The LLM acts as a database that stores every test result permanently so that the front end can query them later on
The LLM acts as a load balancer that distributes test execution across servers without interpreting any of the testware
The LLM acts as a static file server that returns scripted answers from a fixed list of approved responses written by testers

questions.explanation: The LLM is not just a server but a smart processing component that interprets and reasons based on testware, generating test insights dynamically from context such as requirements, code or test results, unlike rule-based chatbots with scripted responses. It is not a load balancer or a result store. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.1 (p. 44); GenAI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: How are relevant chunks selected when a RAG system processes a user query?

options.text: The chunks are retrieved at random, and the LLM discards those that do not seem relevant to the user's question
The query's exact keywords are matched, and chunks that contain all keywords in the same order are retrieved first
The query is encoded, and chunks are retrieved by the semantic similarity between their embeddings and the query's embedding
The newest chunks are retrieved first, because RAG assumes recent documents are the most relevant to any query

questions.explanation: In the retrieval step, the system retrieves relevant information from the vector database based on semantic similarity between the embeddings of the prompt and those of the chunks. It does not rely on exact keyword order, random selection or recency alone. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.2 (p. 45); GenAI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes autonomous from semi-autonomous LLM-powered agents?

options.text: Autonomous agents need a human to approve each tool call; semi-autonomous agents never involve a human after they have been started
Autonomous agents use small language models; semi-autonomous agents use large language models with bigger context windows
Autonomous agents run on the tester's computer; semi-autonomous agents run in the cloud and are managed by the LLM vendor
Autonomous agents work with minimal human intervention; semi-autonomous agents work with periodic human oversight of their output

questions.explanation: Autonomous agents operate independently with minimal human intervention using predefined rules, reinforcement learning and adaptive feedback loops; semi-autonomous agents perform tasks with periodic human oversight to ensure outputs meet user-defined goals. Model size and hosting location do not define the distinction. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.3 (p. 46); GenAI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An organisation wants an LLM to generate test cases from user stories in its own template and terminology. Which approach does the syllabus give as an example of fine-tuning for this purpose?

options.text: Training the model on random internet text so that it forgets the organisation's terms
Training the model on competitors' defect reports and test cases so that it predicts their next releases
Training the model on the organisation's user stories and their corresponding test cases
Training the model on public novels and short stories so that its writing style becomes more varied

questions.explanation: By training the model on the organisation's user stories and corresponding test cases, the model aligns with the organisation's specific test process and terminology. The other datasets are not task-specific or relevant. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 47); GenAI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An organisation plans to use a commercial test tool with built-in GenAI features. Which LLMOps consideration applies in addition to those for using an AI chatbot?

options.text: Removing existing test processes, because a tool with GenAI capabilities replaces rather than complements them
Training all testers as data scientists, because built-in GenAI features require custom model development by users
