Evaluating the data security and performance assurances offered by the test tool provider, with a cost-benefit analysis
Developing its own LLM from scratch, because commercial test tools cannot use externally hosted language models

questions.explanation: Using a test tool with GenAI capabilities shares the chatbot considerations (privacy, security, cost) and adds evaluating the provider's data security and performance assurances; such tools complement existing processes and need a cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment. In-house development and replacing processes are not required. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 48); GenAI-4.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which risk of shadow AI concerns unclear licensing agreements for the AI tools being used?

options.text: Compliance and regulatory issues
Information security weakness
Data poisoning
Vague intellectual property

questions.explanation: Using AI tools with unclear licensing agreements can expose LLM users to intellectual property disputes, especially if copyrighted data is processed without authorisation: the risk of vague intellectual property. The other options are attack vectors or output defects. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Why does the syllabus emphasise data quality in a GenAI strategy for testing?

options.text: Because high-quality input data removes the need to review generated testware, so the quality gates can be dropped from the process
Because LLMs are retrained on each prompt, so poor input data permanently damages the model used by the whole organisation
Because the effectiveness of LLM-powered test work depends on accurate, relevant input data protected by robust security procedures
Because data quality determines the licence fee charged by LLM vendors, so better data lowers the recurring cost of the model

questions.explanation: The effectiveness of LLM-powered testing depends on accurate, relevant input data protected by robust security procedures; high-quality input is key to trustworthy results. LLMs are not retrained on each prompt, licence fees do not depend on data quality, and reviews remain necessary. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why does the syllabus recommend that organisations evaluate LLMs against their own benchmarks for test tasks?

options.text: Because public benchmarks are illegal to use in commercial organisations, so internal benchmarks are the one legal option
Because LLM vendors publish no information about their models, so testers cannot obtain any public measurement
Because many public benchmarks exist for tasks such as code generation, but few focus specifically on software test tasks
Because internal benchmarks guarantee that the chosen model will never hallucinate in production test tasks

questions.explanation: Many benchmarks evaluate LLMs and SLMs for NLP, code generation or image analysis, but only a few focus specifically on software test tasks, so selection requires careful evaluation against the organisation's benchmarks. The other reasons are false. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: In which adoption phase does an organisation train test teams on GenAI concepts, give them access to LLMs and experiment with initial use cases?

options.text: Discovery
Decommissioning and review
Initiation and usage definition
Utilisation and iteration

questions.explanation: The discovery phase focuses on awareness and capability building: training test teams, providing access to LLMs/SLMs and experimenting with initial use cases to build confidence. The later phases prioritise use cases and integrate GenAI fully; decommissioning is not a phase in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements describe skills or knowledge that testers need to work effectively with GenAI? Select TWO.

options.text: Understanding the inherent risks of generative models along with common mitigation strategies
Combining domain and test expertise with AI know-how to evaluate LLM-driven test case generation
Memorising the token prices of all LLM vendors so that costs never need to be estimated
Avoiding any review of AI-generated testware so that the productivity gains are realised
Programming new transformer architectures from scratch for each project the team supports

questions.explanation: Testers must combine domain and test expertise with AI skills to evaluate LLM-driven testing, and essential knowledge includes the inherent risks of GenAI and common mitigations. Building transformers, memorising prices or skipping reviews are not described as needed skills. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which approach does the syllabus recommend for building GenAI capabilities in test teams?

options.text: Hands-on practice with various LLMs and SLMs, structured learning paths and sharing of know-how
A rule that testers learn GenAI in their own free time, without access to any approved LLMs or training material
A policy that external consultants alone use GenAI, so that testers do not need to develop related skills
A one-day lecture on transformer mathematics, followed by an exam that each tester must pass before using GenAI

questions.explanation: Building GenAI capabilities needs a hands-on approach: practising with various LLMs/SLMs, following structured learning paths and gradually developing know-how through sharing, with guided exercises and peer learning. The other approaches are not recommended. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which new task is added to testers' responsibilities in an AI-enabled test organisation?

options.text: Writing the company's AI regulations
Approving the organisation's budget
Negotiating LLM licence contracts
Maintaining test-specific prompt libraries

questions.explanation: Testers' tasks expand to include review of AI-based output, prompt refinement and maintenance of test-specific prompt libraries. Budgets, contracts and regulations are not tester responsibilities in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 53); GenAI-5.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which statement about deep learning is correct?

options.text: It requires users to define every feature manually before training, unlike classical machine learning
It uses neural networks that learn features automatically from large, complex datasets such as images or text
It is a type of generative AI that is limited to producing images from short textual descriptions
It uses explicit if-then rules written by experts, so it needs no training data at any stage of its use

questions.explanation: Deep learning uses neural networks to learn features automatically from very large and complex datasets, without users defining features manually, although humans may still annotate data or validate results. Explicit rules describe symbolic AI, and GenAI builds on deep learning rather than the reverse. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: How does an LLM based on the transformer model generate text during inference?

options.text: It predicts the next token in a sequence, using the relationships between tokens that it learned in training
It applies grammar rules written by linguists to assemble sentences from a dictionary of permitted words
It copies the most frequent paragraph in its training data that contains the words used in the prompt
It retrieves complete sentences from a database of approved answers and returns the closest stored match to the prompt

questions.explanation: Transformer-based LLMs learn how tokens relate to each other and, during inference, predict the next token, generating statistically plausible text. They do not look up stored answers, apply hand-written grammar rules or copy the most frequent paragraph. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An LLM produces a fluent, well-structured set of test cases for a feature. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The output is complete, because the context window ensures that all requirements were considered
The output is statistically plausible text, which is not necessarily correct, so it must be verified
The output is reproducible, because a fluent response shows that the model has reached a stable final answer
The output is correct, because a transformer only generates text that it has verified internally

questions.explanation: Transformer models generate text that is statistically plausible based on training data and the prompt, but plausible is not necessarily correct. LLMs do not verify their own output, may miss requirements and are non-deterministic. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement BEST describes foundation LLMs?

options.text: They are models fine-tuned on prompt-response pairs so that they follow instructions closely in each domain
They are models trained on chain-of-thought tasks so that they solve multi-step technical problems reliably
They are compact models designed for one specific test task, such as classifying defect reports by severity
They are general-purpose models trained on vast, diverse data and typically need further adaptation for specific tasks

questions.explanation: Foundation LLMs are general-purpose models trained on vast, diverse datasets; they are powerful and flexible but usually need adaptation to meet specific requirements. Prompt-response tuning gives instruction-tuned models, chain-of-thought training gives reasoning models, and compact task-specific models are SLMs. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about vision-language models is correct?

options.text: They are a subset of multimodal LLMs that integrate visual and textual information, for example for visual question answering
They are rule-based systems that compare screenshots pixel by pixel with stored reference images of the user interface
They are small language models that can process text alone and are used to label images for supervised training
They are language models that translate spoken test instructions into text, so testers can dictate their test cases

questions.explanation: Vision-language models are a subset of multimodal LLMs that integrate visual and textual information for tasks such as image captioning, visual question answering and checking consistency between text and images. They are not pixel comparison tools, speech-to-text systems or text-only SLMs. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.4 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which example illustrates the test automation support capability of an LLM?

options.text: Generating a test script from a written test case and suggesting improvements to an existing script
Generating a test plan document and updating it as the project scope changes over the course of several sprints
Generating questions for stakeholders about ambiguous wording in a newly written requirement
Generating boundary values and combinations of test data for an input field with stated limits

questions.explanation: Test automation support includes generating test scripts from test case descriptions, improving existing scripts and suggesting appropriate test techniques. The other options describe test data generation, testware creation and requirements analysis. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 17); GenAI-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: For which situation does the syllabus describe AI chatbots as particularly effective?

options.text: Embedding an LLM into a commercial test management tool so that defects are clustered automatically
Operating several coordinated agents that execute the whole test lifecycle without human interaction
Running a fully automated nightly pipeline that generates and executes thousands of test scripts
Onboarding new testers by giving quick access to testing knowledge and clarifying test concepts

questions.explanation: Chatbots are effective for routine tasks, exploratory testing, fast feedback, clarifying test concepts and onboarding new testers, and their intuitive interface suits non-technical stakeholders. Automated pipelines, tool integration and coordinated agents describe LLM-powered applications and agents. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 18); GenAI-1.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which prompt component should contain the user stories, acceptance criteria, screenshots or existing test cases that the LLM needs to perform the task?

options.text: Input data
Context
Role
Constraints

questions.explanation: Input data includes the information needed to perform the task, such as user stories, acceptance criteria, screenshots, code, existing test cases or output examples. Context gives background, the role sets a persona, and constraints restrict how instructions are applied. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt:
A tester's prompt reads:
'You are a test analyst. We are testing the password reset feature of a web portal. Derive test conditions from the acceptance criteria below. Cover only the listed criteria.
AC1: …  AC2: …  AC3: …'
Which component of the six-part structure is missing?

options.text: Role
Output format
Constraints
Instruction

questions.explanation: The prompt has a role (test analyst), context (password reset feature), instruction (derive test conditions), constraints (cover only the listed criteria) and input data (the criteria), but it does not specify the expected format of the response. Adding an output format would shape the result. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester is unsure how to phrase a prompt for analysing performance-test logs. Which technique helps MOST, and why?

options.text: Meta prompting, because you and the LLM can co-create and refine an effective prompt together
Zero-shot prompting, because the model's pre-existing knowledge removes the need to evaluate the prompt
Prompt chaining, because splitting the log into chunks lets the model design the analysis by itself
Few-shot prompting, because examples of analysed logs make the prompt structure unnecessary for the task

questions.explanation: Meta prompting leverages the LLM's ability to generate or refine prompts and is useful when the tester is unsure how to craft an effective prompt, forming a pairing between tester and AI. The other options misstate what their techniques provide. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 22); GenAI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which parts of a structured prompt does the syllabus say a system prompt may contain?

options.text: The full conversation history of all users, so that every new session starts with shared knowledge
Elements such as the role, context and constraints, and general instructions about the expected output
The specific user story to analyse in the current interaction and the expected test conditions for it
The model's weights and hyperparameters, so that the chatbot is retrained at the start of each session

questions.explanation: A system prompt may contain parts of a structured prompt such as the role, context and constraints, and general instructions, for example regarding the expected output. The specific story to analyse belongs in the user prompt, and system prompts do not contain weights or other users' conversations. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 23); GenAI-2.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester has a user story and a GUI wireframe image for a booking form and wants acceptance criteria from a multimodal LLM. Which prompt is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A structured prompt with the story only, asking the model to imagine the screen layout and to add any fields it considers useful
A meta prompt asking the model to write a better user story, then sending the new story to stakeholders without any review step
A one-line prompt asking for 'acceptance criteria for this form', sending the wireframe image without the user story or any context
A structured prompt with role, context, instruction, the story and the wireframe as input data, constraints on fields and business rules, and an output format

questions.explanation: Providing a structured prompt with both textual and image input, explicit constraints such as field rules and business rules, and an output format leads to well-formed, clear and complete acceptance criteria. Omitting inputs or inviting the model to invent fields encourages hallucination, and skipping review is risky. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); GenAI-2.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester must prioritise 25 regression test cases that have dependencies (for example 'create account' must run before 'close account') and risk ratings. Which application of GenAI is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A few-shot prompt with two prioritised suites from other projects, executed without checking the resulting order
One prompt that asks for the optimal order of the dependent cases, accepting the answer because reasoning models do not make ordering mistakes
A prompt chain that first lists dependency chains, then orders cases by risk within those chains, with manual verification of each step
A meta prompt that asks the model to decide which test cases can be deleted so that no prioritisation is needed

questions.explanation: Prioritisation with dependencies needs multi-criteria reasoning, so a prompt chain with manual verification at each step helps detect errors in the LLM's reasoning. Reasoning models can still make mistakes, unchecked output from other projects' examples is risky, and deleting tests avoids the task. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 25); GenAI-2.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: After a UI redesign, many GUI regression scripts fail because element locators changed, although the application behaves correctly. How can GenAI help, and what must the tester still do?

options.text: GenAI can rewrite the application's UI to match the old locators; the tester then reruns the unchanged regression suite
GenAI can mark the failed scripts as passed because the behavior is correct; the tester then deletes the old locator definitions
GenAI can remove all GUI tests and replace them with API tests; the tester then updates the test plan to reflect this
GenAI can adapt the scripts to the new locators (self-healing); the tester checks that they verify the intended behavior

questions.explanation: Self-healing and adaptive tests let GenAI automatically adjust scripts to minor UI or API changes, such as dynamic locators and modified interactions, keeping suites stable. Because GenAI can make mistakes, the tester must check the adapted scripts. Marking failures as passed, changing the application or dropping GUI tests are inappropriate. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 27); GenAI-2.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: At the end of a release, a test manager wants a test completion report. How can GenAI BEST support this task?

options.text: By deleting the test data after the report is drafted, because completion reports should not refer to the underlying test results
By drafting the completion report from the collected test data, highlighting successes and lessons learned for review by the team
By rewriting the release requirements so that the open defects no longer violate any acceptance criteria for the release
By approving the release on behalf of stakeholders, because the completion report already contains all relevant test data

questions.explanation: GenAI can assist by generating test completion reports that highlight successes and lessons learned, helping teams refine strategies and improve future processes. Approving releases, deleting data or rewriting requirements are not appropriate tasks for GenAI. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.4 (p. 28); GenAI-2.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team has never used GenAI to detect anomalies in performance-test reports and does not know how to phrase a good prompt. Which prompting technique fits this situation BEST?

options.text: Meta prompting
Few-shot prompting
Prompt chaining
Zero-shot prompting

questions.explanation: Meta prompting suits flexible, dynamic tasks and crafting prompts for new tasks: a general description of the objective guides the LLM in creating the prompt, useful for complex tasks such as test report analysis and anomaly detection. The team lacks examples for few-shot prompting and a defined step sequence for chaining. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.5 (p. 29); GenAI-2.2.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: For a 'payment amount' data class, the team identified 12 valid and invalid equivalence partitions. The generated test cases exercise 9 of them. Which metric does the syllabus associate with this example?

options.text: Diversity
Recall
Precision
Accuracy

questions.explanation: The syllabus describes recall as the ability to identify all relevant instances, with the example of how far generated test cases cover the valid and invalid equivalence partitions of a data class; here 9 of 12 (75%). Precision, diversity and accuracy are described with other examples. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.1 (p. 31); GenAI-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester notices that generated test cases repeatedly contradict the test basis in the same way. Which refinement technique addresses this MOST directly?

options.text: Temperature tuning: increasing randomness so that the same contradiction does not appear in two consecutive runs
Diversity: asking for more varied test cases, which makes the contradictions with the test basis less visible
Output analysis: examining the inaccuracies and their types to improve the prompt and avoid similar defects
Time efficiency: measuring how much faster the model is than a tester, which shows the defects are acceptable

questions.explanation: Output analysis examines AI-generated output for inaccuracies or inconsistencies, for example with respect to the test basis; understanding the types of errors helps refine prompts to avoid similar defects. The other options do not address the cause and may hide the problem. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.2 (p. 32); GenAI-2.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Where do biases in LLM output originate, according to the CT-GenAI syllabus?

options.text: From the data on which the model was trained
From the size of the context window
From the tester's choice of output format
From the temperature setting used at inference

questions.explanation: LLM biases originate from the data on which the model was trained and can lead to outputs that favour certain information, approaches or assumptions, for example underrepresenting non-English perspectives. Temperature, output format and context window size are not given as the source. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A global travel app is sold in 30 countries. An LLM generates 500 synthetic traveller profiles for testing, and all names, addresses and phone formats come from one country. The test strategy requires coverage of international formats. What does this MOST LIKELY indicate, and how should it be detected?

options.text: A hallucination in the generated test data, detected by running the profiles through the app to measure the coverage the strategy requires
Non-determinism in the generated test data, detected by repeating the prompt until profiles from other countries appear
Bias in the generated test data, detected by reviewing whether the data represents the test strategy and coverage requirements
A reasoning error in the generated test data, detected by checking the arithmetic of the 500 profile identifiers

questions.explanation: A systematic skew toward one population reflects bias inherited from training data; bias detection reviews whether generated testware fairly and accurately represents the defined test strategy and coverage requirements. The profiles are not invented facts or logic errors, and repeating prompts does not address bias. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team pastes test data into prompts as unformatted text copied from a spreadsheet, and the LLM often confuses the columns. Which mitigation fits BEST?

options.text: Use the system prompt for the data, so that the columns become invisible to the end users
Use a smaller context window, so that the model reads fewer columns of the pasted data
Use clear, interpretable data formats, such as a structured table with labelled columns
Use a random seed, so that the model confuses the same columns in each repeated response

questions.explanation: Avoiding ambiguous formats and using structured, straightforward formats helps the model focus on the essential aspects of the task. A smaller window, a seed or moving the data to the system prompt does not make the data easier to interpret. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: How can setting a random seed help when using LLMs for test tasks?

options.text: The system prompt is regenerated randomly, which increases the diversity of the generated test cases
The context window is reset to its initial state, which removes the effect of the earlier prompts entirely
Where the implementation allows it, the same pseudo-random sequence is used, which improves reproducibility
The model is retrained with a new seed dataset, which removes hallucinations from subsequent answers

questions.explanation: Some LLM implementations allow setting a seed for the random number generator, so the same pseudo-random sequence is used, improving reproducibility. Seeds do not retrain the model, reset the context window or regenerate system prompts. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.4 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which security risk specific to testing with GenAI does the syllabus describe?

options.text: Developers may read generated test cases, which reveals the expected results of the system tests
Test managers may use dashboards produced by GenAI, which exposes the test plan to security threats online
Attackers may introduce malicious input data to mislead LLMs and compromise their accuracy or security
Testers may write prompts that are too long, which causes the LLM vendor to suspend their accounts

questions.explanation: Security risks include attacks on LLM-powered test infrastructure, exploitation of LLM vulnerabilities such as manipulative attacks, and attackers introducing malicious input data to mislead LLMs. The other options are not security risks in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt:
Given these attack vectors:
1. Context manipulation
2. Request manipulation
3. Data poisoning
4. Malicious code generation
And these examples:
A. Testers rate generated test reports with deliberately false scores that are used to improve the tool
B. A generated test script includes a hidden call that sends data to an external server
C. A prompt with an extremely long input makes the model output fragments of its training data
D. A misleading image in the prompt leads the model to describe criteria for a different feature
Which matching is BEST?
questions.explanation: Extracting training data fragments through an overloaded context is context manipulation; a misleading image is request manipulation; false ratings used for improvement are data poisoning; a hidden external call is malicious code generation. Each distractor swaps at least two pairs. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An attacker wants an LLM-powered test assistant to reveal confidential information from its training data. Which approach corresponds to the context manipulation vector described in the syllabus?

options.text: Requesting test scripts that include command calls so that the generated code opens a channel to the attacker
Submitting extremely long prompts that exceed the context window so that the model outputs random snippets of training data
Uploading screenshots with misleading visual cues into the context so that the assistant hallucinates criteria for another application
Submitting false ratings of the assistant's reports so that later training runs favour the attacker's preferences

questions.explanation: Context manipulation sends requests designed to extract confidential training data, for example by exceeding the context window with long prompts so the model reveals random snippets. The other options describe request manipulation, data poisoning and malicious code generation. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A company wants to use GenAI on highly confidential test documents. Which TWO mitigation strategies does the syllabus describe? Select TWO.

options.text: Disabling human review of generated output so that fewer people can see the confidential test documents
Raising the temperature so that generated outputs are too random to reveal any confidential information
Choosing a secure environment, such as a commercial secure offering, a secure cloud or an LLM on its own infrastructure
Publishing the confidential documents so that the LLM provider can train its models on accurate data
Performing regular security audits and vulnerability assessments of the LLM-powered systems used for testing

questions.explanation: Choosing a secure operational environment and regular security audits and vulnerability assessments are among the listed mitigations, with systematic review, comparison with another LLM, data minimisation, anonymisation, secure storage and training. The distractors increase risk or misuse settings. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 39); GenAI-3.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which factors influence the energy consumption of GenAI in software testing, according to the syllabus?

options.text: The length of the test plan and the day of the week on which the prompts are submitted to the model
The programming language of the system under test and the number of open defects in the defect tracker
The number of testers in the team and the colour scheme of the chatbot interface used to send the prompts
The complexity of the task and the computational resources it requires, together with how often models are used

questions.explanation: Energy consumption rises sharply as usage increases and depends on the complexity of the task and the computational resources required. Team size, interface colours, programming language or the day of the week are not the factors described. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.3.1 (p. 40); GenAI-3.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item is a US publication offering guidelines for managing AI risks, with a focus on fairness, transparency and security?

options.text: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 management system standard
EU Artificial Intelligence Act
NIST AI Risk Management Framework

questions.explanation: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (US) offers guidelines for managing AI risks focusing on fairness, transparency and security. The other items are a management system standard, an EU regulation and a framework standard for ML-based AI systems. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.4.1 (p. 41); GenAI-3.4.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which data sources does the syllabus mention that the back end of an LLM-powered test infrastructure can integrate?

options.text: Spreadsheets edited by testers in their browsers, and email inboxes that collect messages from stakeholders
Printed test plans scanned by an assistant, and voice recordings of daily stand-up meetings of the test team
Source-code repositories of competitors, and social media feeds that report production incidents in real time
Relational databases for structured data such as test cases, and vector databases for semantic retrieval using embeddings

questions.explanation: The back end integrates multiple data sources, such as relational databases for structured data used in testing (for example test cases) and vector databases for semantic retrieval of related content using embeddings. The other options are not mentioned. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.1 (p. 44); GenAI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of RAG for LLM-powered test infrastructure?

options.text: It removes the need for an LLM, because retrieved document chunks are shown to testers directly as the final answer to their query
It makes the LLM deterministic, because retrieved chunks replace the probabilistic sampling of tokens during response generation
It changes the LLM's weights after each query, so that the model gradually memorises the organisation's specifications
It lets the LLM use enterprise data sources such as documentation and repositories in real time, aligning test tasks with current specifications

questions.explanation: RAG enables LLM-powered test infrastructure to access enterprise data sources such as databases, documentation and repositories in real time, so test analysis or design aligns with the latest specifications, requirements and test data. The LLM still generates the response, sampling remains probabilistic, and weights are unchanged. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.2 (p. 45); GenAI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about LLM-powered agents in test automation are consistent with the syllabus? Select TWO.

options.text: Agents remove the need for test analysis, because they execute tests without any test basis
Agents are deterministic, because tool calls replace the probabilistic behavior of the LLM
Multi-agent architectures coordinate several specialised agents, which is known as orchestration
Agents can only be used for test reporting, because they cannot interact with external systems
Agents can hallucinate or make reasoning errors, so their results need verification for critical tasks

questions.explanation: Several specialised agents communicating and coordinating is orchestration, and agents suffer from the same hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases as LLMs, mitigated by automated verification or semi-autonomous agents for critical tasks. Agents still rely on a test basis, are not deterministic, and can act on external systems. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.3 (p. 46); GenAI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which challenge of fine-tuning a language model for software testing does the syllabus describe as overfitting?

options.text: The model forgets the prompt structure, so the six prompt components can no longer be used
The model becomes too specialised to its training data and performs poorly on new, unseen data
The model needs so little computing power that it can no longer run on dedicated servers
The model becomes so transparent that its reviewers can no longer follow its long explanations

questions.explanation: Overfitting means the model becomes too specialised to the training data, negatively affecting its performance on new data; mitigating it maintains generalisation. The other statements do not describe overfitting; the syllabus mentions opacity, not excessive transparency, as a challenge. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 47); GenAI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which LLMOps approach gives an organisation the most comprehensive control over data privacy and security risks?

options.text: In-house development of a test tool based on generative AI
Using a commercial test tool with GenAI features
Using a public AI chatbot with the default settings
Using an LLM-as-a-Service without vendor assurances

questions.explanation: In-house development of a GenAI-based test tool emphasises comprehensive control of data privacy and security risks, but needs careful planning of resources, structured validation and maintenance processes and expertise. The other approaches depend on external providers. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 48); GenAI-4.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which list gives the risks of shadow AI described in the syllabus?

options.text: Hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases that appear only in unapproved tools and never in approved ones
Higher test coverage, faster test cycles and lower recurring costs for each team that uses its own tools
Information security and data privacy weaknesses, compliance and regulatory issues, and vague intellectual property
Longer context windows, larger embeddings and slower inference compared with approved organisational tools

questions.explanation: Shadow AI can lead to information security and data privacy weaknesses, compliance and regulatory issues, and vague intellectual property. The other lists describe benefits, output defects that affect all tools, or technical properties. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which process guideline belongs in a GenAI strategy to ensure compliance and ethical use?

options.text: Rules forbidding the collection of metrics on GenAI results, so that teams are not discouraged by early measurements of quality
Rules for the use of sensitive data, transparency about what was generated with GenAI, and quality gates with review of generated testware
Rules requiring that generated testware is released without review, so that teams obtain the productivity benefits of GenAI quickly
Rules allowing testers to keep their prompts private, so that generated testware cannot be traced back to any particular GenAI tool

questions.explanation: Process guidelines should include rules for using sensitive data, transparency obligations (for example what was generated using GenAI) and quality gates with review of generated testware. Hiding origin, skipping reviews or avoiding metrics contradict the strategy. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which selection criterion considers licensing fees and operational expenses of using an LLM for the targeted test tasks?

options.text: Model performance
Recurring cost
Community and support
Fine-tuning potential

questions.explanation: Recurring cost considers the ongoing costs of using the LLM or SLM, including licensing fees and operational expenses, so that it fits the organisation's budget for the targeted test tasks. The other criteria concern quality, adaptability and support. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: In which adoption phase does an organisation fully integrate GenAI into its test processes with continuous monitoring and measurement of the transformation?

options.text: Discovery
Initiation and usage definition
Pilot and procurement
Utilisation and iteration

questions.explanation: In the utilisation and iteration phase, organisations fully integrate GenAI into their test processes, with continuous monitoring of progress and tools and measurement and management of the transformation. Discovery builds awareness, initiation defines use cases, and 'pilot and procurement' is not a syllabus phase. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which environmental consideration does the syllabus include among the skills needed for testing with GenAI?

options.text: Selecting models hosted in cold climates, because data-centre cooling is the main factor in GenAI energy use
Selecting right-sized models for test tasks and balancing the benefits of GenAI automation with cost and energy consumption
Selecting the largest available model for each task, because larger models use energy more efficiently
Selecting models without any context window, because context windows are the main source of CO2 emissions

questions.explanation: Environmental considerations include optimising model selection and usage patterns to reduce computational overhead, selecting right-sized models for test tasks and balancing GenAI automation benefits with the impact on cost and energy. The other claims are not in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of internal communities of practice for GenAI in test organisations?

options.text: To support ongoing knowledge sharing, highlight successful applications, discuss challenges and refine ways of working
To approve each prompt before it is sent to an LLM, so that no tester can use GenAI without the community's vote
To negotiate licence prices with vendors, so that each community can buy its own GenAI tool independently of others
To replace formal training programs, so that the organisation no longer needs any structured learning paths for its testers

questions.explanation: Internal communities of practice support ongoing knowledge sharing, with regular meetings to highlight successful GenAI applications, discuss challenges and refine best practices, sharing prompt pattern libraries and lessons learned. They do not approve each prompt, replace training or buy tools. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which responsibility is added for those who lead test teams when adopting GenAI?

options.text: Writing each prompt that the testers send to the language model
Replacing human reviews of testware with decisions taken by test agents
Developing an AI-based test strategy and AI-based risk management
Training the organisation's language models from scratch

questions.explanation: Test managers' responsibilities are updated to include developing an AI-based test strategy, AI-based risk management, and monitoring and control of AI-based test processes. They do not write every prompt, train models from scratch or replace reviews with agents. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 53); GenAI-5.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: According to the CT-GenAI syllabus, what is the key advantage of using generative AI for software testing compared with other types of AI?

options.text: Generated outputs are deterministic, so the same prompt gives the same set of test cases each time
Generated outputs need no input data, so no test basis has to be provided in the prompts
Generated outputs are correct by design, so testers no longer need to review the testware
Pre-trained models can be applied directly to test tasks without an additional training phase

questions.explanation: The key advantage of GenAI for testing is that pre-trained models can be applied directly to test tasks without an extra training phase, although this brings risks. LLM outputs are non-deterministic and can be wrong, and prompts still need relevant input data. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What effect does a larger context window have on an LLM?

options.text: It lowers computational complexity, because the model needs fewer passes to read the long passages of input text given
It makes the model deterministic, because more context removes the randomness from next-token prediction
It enlarges the model's training dataset, because every prompt inside the window is learned permanently
It lets the model keep coherence over longer passages, but increases computational complexity and processing time

questions.explanation: A larger context window allows the model to maintain coherence over longer passages, such as large test logs, but increases computational complexity and processing time. It does not make output deterministic or add prompts to the training data. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is a small language model (SLM)?

options.text: A model that has been trained on test cases alone, so it cannot be used for any other software engineering task
A rule-based chatbot that uses a small dictionary of approved phrases instead of a neural network architecture
A compact model with fewer parameters than an LLM, designed to provide lightweight and focused GenAI solutions
A large language model that has been restricted to answering short prompts of fewer than one hundred tokens

questions.explanation: SLMs are compact models with fewer parameters than LLMs, designed for lightweight and focused GenAI solutions; they can be fine-tuned for specific tasks with less computational overhead. They are not prompt-length restrictions, rule-based chatbots or models limited to test cases by definition. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does the syllabus describe the choice between instruction-tuned and reasoning LLMs for testing?

options.text: Reasoning LLMs replace instruction-tuned LLMs for all test tasks, because they make fewer errors in any context
Neither is used in testing, because test tasks need foundation LLMs that have not been tuned for instructions
Both are used in testing, and the selection depends on the complexity and reasoning demands of the test task
Instruction-tuned LLMs are preferred for all test tasks, because reasoning LLMs are designed for mathematics

questions.explanation: Both instruction-tuned (sometimes called non-reasoning) and reasoning LLMs are used for GenAI testing applications; the selection depends on the complexity and reasoning demands of the specific test task. Neither type is universally preferred. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: How can LLMs augmented with vision-language models increase test coverage?

options.text: By generating test cases that combine textual data with visual cues taken from screenshots or wireframes
By measuring code coverage from screenshots of the integrated development environment during test runs
By removing duplicate test cases whose screenshots look identical, which raises the overall coverage percentage
By executing test cases directly on the screen and replacing the need for test automation frameworks

questions.explanation: LLMs augmented with vision-language models can generate rich, realistic test cases that incorporate both textual data and visual cues, increasing overall coverage. They do not replace automation frameworks, measure code coverage from images or raise coverage by deleting tests. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.4 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about LLM capabilities across the test process is consistent with the syllabus?

options.text: LLMs can support test management alone, because generating testware such as test cases is reserved for automation tools
LLMs can support test execution alone, because analysis and design need human judgement that models cannot provide in a useful form
LLMs can support documentation tasks alone, because they cannot process code, screenshots or structured test results reliably
LLMs can interpret requirements, screenshots, code, test cases and defect reports, so they can support activities throughout the test process

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that LLMs can interpret requirements, specifications, screenshots, code, test cases and defect reports and can affect many aspects of testing through the whole test process. They are not limited to execution, documentation or management. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 17); GenAI-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does the syllabus say is required for success regardless of whether testers use chatbots or LLM-powered testing applications?

options.text: Strong prompt engineering, with carefully designed prompts and clear, specific instructions
A reasoning LLM, because instruction-tuned models cannot be used for any test tasks
A fine-tuned model, because pre-trained models cannot produce output relevant to tests
A vector database, because LLMs cannot answer prompts that contain no retrieved context from documents

questions.explanation: Whatever the interaction model, successful use of GenAI in testing requires strong prompt engineering; carefully designed prompts with clear, specific instructions improve accuracy and relevance. Reasoning models, fine-tuning and RAG can help but are not stated as universal requirements. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 18); GenAI-1.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the constraints component of a structured prompt?

options.text: To describe the persona and tone that the LLM should adopt while it performs the requested task given in the prompt
To define the expected structure and characteristics of the response, such as a table with named columns
To state restrictions or special considerations that specify how the instructions are applied to the input data
To provide the background information the LLM needs, such as the test object and the functionality to test

questions.explanation: Constraints outline restrictions or special considerations the LLM should adhere to and specify how instructions are applied to the input data. Persona is the role, background is context, and response structure is the output format. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: How should the six-component prompt structure be used in practice, according to the syllabus?

options.text: As the basic structure of a prompt, combined with a prompting technique chosen for the task and the LLM in use
As a template for system prompts alone, because user prompts must contain instructions and nothing else
As a checklist for reviewing outputs, because the six components describe the parts of a good LLM response
As a replacement for prompting techniques, because a complete structure makes chaining or examples unnecessary

questions.explanation: The six components form the basic structure of the prompt, which should be combined with prompting techniques depending on the task and the LLM. The structure does not replace techniques, is not limited to system prompts, and describes the prompt rather than the response. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the main characteristic of prompt chaining?

options.text: A task is sent in parallel to several LLMs, and the response that appears most often is selected as the answer
A task is described in general terms so that the LLM writes the detailed prompt that the tester then executes
A task is described once in a single long prompt that contains every example and constraint that the model might need
A task is broken into a series of intermediate prompts, and each result is checked and refined before the next step

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining involves breaking a task into intermediate steps (multiple prompts), checking and refining each result before proceeding, which increases accuracy. A single long prompt is not chaining, comparing several LLMs is a mitigation technique, and having the LLM write the prompt is meta prompting. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 22); GenAI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team builds a test-review assistant. Which text should be placed in the system prompt rather than in a user prompt?

options.text: You review test cases using ISTQB terminology, answer concisely and flag any uncertainty explicitly.
Here is today's regression report; summarise the failures that are new since yesterday's run.
Review these five test cases against acceptance criterion AC-3 and list all of the gaps as bullet points.
Compare test case TC-17 with the updated user story and suggest changes to its expected results.

questions.explanation: Rules that guide behavior for the whole conversation, such as terminology, tone and how to handle uncertainty, belong in the system prompt, which stays constant. Task-specific requests with their input data change per interaction and belong in user prompts. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 23); GenAI-2.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An LLM generated 40 test conditions from 14 requirements. The tester wants to know whether any requirement aspect lacks a test condition. Which GenAI-supported test analysis task should the tester apply next?

options.text: Test execution scheduling, ordering the 40 generated conditions by their dependencies and priorities
Coverage analysis, mapping each requirement to the generated test conditions to reveal gaps
Test data synthesis, creating privacy-preserving records for each of the 40 test conditions
Defect analysis of the test basis, looking for ambiguous wording in the 14 requirements

questions.explanation: Supporting coverage analysis means mapping requirements and user stories to test conditions to determine whether all aspects of the test basis are covered. Scheduling and data synthesis are design and implementation tasks, and self-healing applies to automated test scripts. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); GenAI-2.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester wants an LLM to generate automated test scripts from structured manual test cases for the team's existing automation framework. Which input is MOST important to include in the prompt?

options.text: The production database password, so that the generated scripts can connect to real data during execution
The names of the developers who wrote the code, so that the model can adapt the scripts to their personal coding style
The project's budget and schedule, so that the model can decide how many scripts are worth generating
The test steps plus the tool's conventions, such as available page objects or keywords, and one example script

questions.explanation: GenAI can translate structured test cases into scripts compatible with test automation frameworks; giving the test cases and the framework's conventions with an example improves compatibility. Budget and developer names do not help, and sharing production credentials is a security risk. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 25); GenAI-2.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester must analyse a regression test report with 300 failures. Which use of structured prompts in a single conversation is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Ask the model to rerun the regression suite with a higher temperature, so that the random failures disappear
Ask the model to declare which failures are product defects, and file all of them as defects without any further review
Compare the results with the test specification, cluster similar failures, update the known-anomalies list, then cross-check the findings
Ask the model to delete the failing tests from the suite, so that the next regression report shows a higher pass rate

questions.explanation: A methodical approach analyses results against the test specification, clusters similar defects, maintains a known-anomalies list and cross-checks findings, linking each step in one conversation. Filing unreviewed output, deleting failing tests or changing temperature do not support sound regression analysis. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 27); GenAI-2.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Business stakeholders find the team's test metrics hard to understand. Which use of GenAI addresses this MOST directly?

options.text: Hiding the defect metrics from stakeholders, so that only the pass rate is visible in the weekly status meeting
Replacing all metrics with a single traffic-light colour chosen by the LLM without access to the underlying data
Generating additional test cases, so that the pass rate increases before the metrics are shown to stakeholders
Creating dynamic dashboards and natural-language summaries of the relevant metrics for each stakeholder group

questions.explanation: GenAI can assist in creating dynamic dashboards and natural-language summaries so that all stakeholders have access to the relevant metrics and a clear view of test progress. Hiding metrics, inflating pass rates or replacing data with an unsupported colour mislead stakeholders. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.4 (p. 28); GenAI-2.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester designs a GenAI workflow for a new test-reporting task. Which combination of techniques does the syllabus describe as possible for a single use case?

options.text: Few-shot prompting to generate the final report, followed by meta prompting to remove the need for any human review
One prompt per technique sent to different LLMs at the same time, keeping the answer that most models agree with
Zero-shot prompting to avoid examples, a higher temperature to vary results, and deletion of intermediate outputs to save tokens
Meta prompting to create an initial prompt, few-shot examples to adapt and enhance it, and prompt chaining to validate intermediate steps

questions.explanation: The syllabus notes that multiple techniques can be used for one use case: meta prompting to create an initial prompt, few-shot prompting to adapt and enhance it with examples, and prompt chaining to divide the task and validate intermediate steps. The other options remove verification or misuse the techniques. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.5 (p. 29); GenAI-2.2.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about evaluating GenAI results on test tasks are correct? Select TWO.

options.text: Metrics can be evaluated by manual review or automated comparison with a predefined reference
One evaluation run is sufficient because an LLM gives the same answer to repeated prompts
Task-specific metrics are not allowed because only the general metrics are reliable for testing
Metrics must be based on statistically relevant data because LLM output is non-deterministic
Execution success rate shows how many defects the generated test cases will detect in production

questions.explanation: Testers may evaluate metrics through manual review or automate them by comparing output with a predefined reference, and because GenAI is non-deterministic, metrics must be based on statistically relevant data. Task-specific metrics are encouraged, and execution success rate concerns whether artefacts run, not defect detection. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.1 (p. 31); GenAI-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why does the syllabus recommend sharing prompt practices and prompt libraries across a test organisation?

options.text: To reduce the need for test basis documents, because shared prompts contain the requirements of all projects
To replace prompt evaluation sessions, because a shared library proves that its prompts work for every future task
To allow each tester to keep private prompts, so that individual results cannot be compared across the organisation
To standardise prompting techniques, maintain consistent quality and build on collective insights instead of repeating errors

questions.explanation: Sharing practices across a team or organisation helps standardise prompt techniques, maintain consistent quality, promote a learning culture and avoid repeated errors, for example by sharing prompt libraries. It does not replace evaluation sessions or test basis documents. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.2 (p. 32); GenAI-2.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why does the syllabus say that LLMs are prone to reasoning errors in tasks such as test planning and test case prioritisation?

options.text: LLMs refuse to answer planning questions, because their system prompts forbid management tasks
LLMs have no access to the test plan, so they cannot read any planning information at all
LLMs lack true logical thinking and rely on pattern matching, which can lead to faulty logic
LLMs store earlier test plans permanently, so they repeat old priorities instead of new ones

questions.explanation: Unlike humans, LLMs lack true logical reasoning and rely on pattern matching, which can lead to faulty logic in tasks that require reasoning, such as mathematical reasoning, test planning and test case prioritisation. The other statements are not reasons given in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: An LLM generated test cases for a new insurance product, and a tester suspects that some refer to policy rules that do not exist. Which detection approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Output testing of the test cases by counting their words, because hallucinated test cases are longer than valid ones
Lowering the temperature and regenerating once, because a lower temperature removes all hallucinated policy rules
Cross-verification of the test cases against the insurer's documentation and requirements, with input from a domain expert
Asking the same LLM whether its test cases are correct, because the model can confirm its own policy knowledge

questions.explanation: Hallucination detection uses cross-verification with existing documentation, requirements and known system behavior, consultation with domain experts and consistency checks. Word counts are meaningless, lower temperature reduces variability but does not remove hallucinations, and self-confirmation is not independent verification. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: For an important test-planning task, a tester runs the same prompt with two different LLMs and compares the outputs. Which mitigation technique is this?

options.text: Comparing results across models to detect output errors and select the most reliable result
Prompt chaining across two models so that the second model compares and executes the plan of the first
Retrieval-augmented generation, because the second model retrieves the output of the first
Fine-tuning both models on the planning data so that they always produce identical results

questions.explanation: Evaluating a prompt with several LLMs and comparing outputs helps detect output errors and select the most reliable results. Fine-tuning, chaining a plan into execution and RAG are different techniques. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the reproducibility of LLM outputs is correct according to the syllabus?

options.text: Complete reproducibility is achieved with a temperature of zero, so verification of generated testware becomes unnecessary
Complete reproducibility is achieved by writing longer prompts, because long outputs are less variable than short outputs
Complete reproducibility cannot be guaranteed, although strategies such as lower temperature and random seeds reduce variability
Complete reproducibility is achieved by using reasoning models, because chain-of-thought removes probabilistic sampling

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that complete reproducibility cannot be guaranteed, while adjusting temperature and setting random seeds reduce variability; automating parts of output verification helps. Long outputs increase the risk of variability, and reasoning models still sample probabilistically. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.4 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Why can LLM-powered test infrastructure be a target of security attacks?

options.text: It can be vulnerable to data breaches or unauthorised access, and attackers can exploit LLM vulnerabilities to extract sensitive information
It runs on public networks alone, so firewalls and access controls cannot be applied to its front-end components
It is maintained by testers rather than administrators, so it cannot receive the security patches its vendor publishes
It stores test results in plain text by design, so the syllabus treats LLM-powered test tools as already compromised by attacks

questions.explanation: LLM-powered test infrastructure can be vulnerable to security attacks such as data breaches or unauthorised access, and malicious actors can exploit LLM vulnerabilities to alter behavior or extract sensitive information. The other claims are not made by the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which attack vector aims to make an LLM produce code containing a backdoor, such as an external command call?

options.text: Data poisoning
Context manipulation
Request manipulation
Malicious code generation

questions.explanation: Malicious code generation manipulates an LLM to generate backdoors, such as external command calls, during use. Request manipulation disrupts outputs with misleading inputs, context manipulation tries to extract training data, and data poisoning manipulates training data. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test tool improves its report generator using testers' ratings. A group of users systematically gives the best reports the lowest ratings. Which attack vector is this?

options.text: Malicious code generation
Data poisoning
Context manipulation
Request manipulation

questions.explanation: Providing fake evaluations when rating the results of an AI-generated test report manipulates the data used to train or improve the model, which is data poisoning. The other vectors concern extracting training data, disruptive inputs and backdoors. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Who does the syllabus recommend involving when defining data privacy and security measures for GenAI in testing?

options.text: The newest testers in the team, because they are most familiar with the latest GenAI chatbot interfaces
The LLM vendor's marketing team, because they know the model's security capabilities better than internal experts
The end users of the product, because they decide which of their data may be pasted into test prompts
Senior security engineers, legal counsel, the CTO or the CISO, where these roles exist in the organisation

questions.explanation: The syllabus highly recommends involving senior security engineers, legal counsel, the CTO or the CISO, if present. Vendor marketing, junior testers or end users are not the recommended decision makers for these measures. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 39); GenAI-3.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team asks a large multimodal model to describe all 3,000 UI screenshots every night, although only the screens changed by the day's commits need checking. Which best practice from the syllabus would reduce the environmental impact MOST directly?

options.text: Adding more context to each prompt, so that the model analyses each screenshot more thoroughly than before
Running the job twice, so that the two sets of descriptions can be compared for non-deterministic output
Increasing the temperature, so that the model produces shorter and more varied screenshot descriptions
Limiting unnecessary model interactions, for example analysing just the affected screenshots

questions.explanation: Adopting best practices such as limiting unnecessary model interactions is critical to mitigating the environmental risks posed by GenAI; here, only changed screens need analysis. Higher temperature, duplicate runs or more context per prompt would not reduce, and could increase, energy use. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.3.1 (p. 40); GenAI-3.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which standard provides a framework for AI systems using machine learning, emphasising lifecycle processes, safety and transparency?

options.text: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
EU AI Act

questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 23053:2022 provides a framework for AI lifecycle processes for systems using machine learning, emphasising safety and transparency. ISO/IEC 42001 concerns AI management systems, the NIST AI RMF is a risk framework and the EU AI Act is a regulation. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.4.1 (p. 41); GenAI-3.4.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Why does the back end of an LLM-powered test infrastructure post-process the LLM's raw output?

options.text: To make sure the responses align with the test conditions in use before they are presented in the front end
To delay the responses so that testers do not send too many prompts to the LLM within a short period of time
To translate the responses into the tester's native language because LLMs can generate answers in English alone
To remove all numbers from the responses because LLMs cannot generate numerical test data that is correct

questions.explanation: The back end enhances the LLM's raw output through post-processing so that responses align with the test conditions of the test process before they reach the front end. The other purposes are not described and rest on false assumptions. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.1 (p. 44); GenAI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why are documents typically split into small chunks (for example 256-512 tokens) in a RAG system?

options.text: To avoid embeddings, because small chunks can be searched without numerical vectors
To make the documents unreadable to attackers, because small chunks cannot be reassembled
To reduce the cost of training, because the LLM is retrained on each chunk separately
To keep retrieval focused and to make the retrieved content compatible with the model's context window

questions.explanation: Chunking ensures focused retrieval and compatibility with the model's context window. It is not a security measure, does not retrain the LLM, and chunks are still encoded into embeddings. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.2 (p. 45); GenAI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does the syllabus describe the effect of AI assistants built on LLM-powered agents in modern testing tools?

options.text: They restrict automation to unit tests written by developers, because agents cannot work with user stories or written requirements
They shift test automation from script-based execution toward goal-driven, agent-based automation across the test lifecycle
They replace the need for test environments, because agents execute tests inside the LLM rather than on test objects
They limit test automation to recording and replaying user sessions, because agents cannot design new tests at all

questions.explanation: AI assistants built on LLM-powered agents can automate activities across the test lifecycle, transforming user stories or requirements into test artefacts, and shift test automation from script-based execution to goal-driven, agent-based automation. The other statements contradict the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.3 (p. 46); GenAI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why might a team fine-tune a small language model (SLM) rather than an LLM for a specific test task?

options.text: An SLM needs no training data, so fine-tuning it avoids the cost of preparing high-quality datasets
A fine-tuned SLM can reach high performance on a narrow task without the computational overhead of an LLM
An SLM has a larger context window than any LLM, so it can process all test artefacts in one prompt
An SLM cannot hallucinate, so its fine-tuned output never needs review by the testers who use it

questions.explanation: SLMs are less resource-intensive, and fine-tuning an SLM can achieve higher performance for specific tasks without the computational overhead required for LLMs. SLMs can still make mistakes, do not have larger context windows by definition, and fine-tuning needs high-quality data. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 47); GenAI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the three approaches to using GenAI in test processes (AI chatbot, test tool with GenAI capabilities, in-house development) is correct?

options.text: They exclude RAG and fine-tuning, which are available only to LLM vendors and not to testers
They are stages of a fixed sequence, so an organisation must use a chatbot before buying a tool
They are not mutually exclusive and can be combined, and they can incorporate RAG and fine-tuning
They are mutually exclusive, so an organisation must choose one single approach for all of its testing

questions.explanation: The approaches are not mutually exclusive: an organisation might use a chatbot for some tasks while developing custom tools for others, and they can incorporate RAG and fine-tuning. They are not a fixed sequence, and RAG and fine-tuning are available to organisations. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 48); GenAI-4.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What helps a test organisation avoid the risks of shadow AI?

options.text: A rule that testers may use any free tool they prefer
A strategy and defined steps for integrating and deploying GenAI
A ban on mentioning GenAI in test plans and test reports
A decision to postpone all testing until regulations settle

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that a strategy and steps for integrating and deploying GenAI can help test organisations avoid shadow AI. Banning mentions or allowing any tool would increase unmanaged use, and postponing testing is not proposed. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which TWO elements belong to a GenAI strategy for software testing according to the syllabus? Select TWO.

options.text: Metrics collected to measure the effectiveness of GenAI results on test tasks
Comprehensive training programs covering technical and ethical skills for the test teams
A rule that generated testware replaces the test basis once it has been approved
A commitment to use the largest available model for every task regardless of cost
A policy that each tester selects and pays for an individual GenAI tool privately

questions.explanation: A GenAI strategy includes measurable objectives, LLM selection, data quality, comprehensive training programs for technical and ethical skills, metrics measuring the effectiveness of GenAI results, and process guidelines. Using the largest model regardless of cost, private tools or replacing the test basis contradict it. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team must choose between two models with similar performance on its benchmarks. One has many active users who share solutions, and detailed documentation; the other has neither. Which selection criterion favours the first model?

options.text: Model performance
Recurring cost
Community and support
Context window size

questions.explanation: Choosing models with active community support and detailed documentation aids implementation and troubleshooting: the community and support criterion. Performance is similar here, cost is not described, and context window size is a technical feature rather than one of the listed criteria. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the adoption phases is correct?

options.text: The phases must be completed in strict sequence for the whole organisation before any use case can move forward
The phases apply to test managers alone, because testers do not participate in adopting GenAI in their organisation
The phases can run in parallel for different use cases, for example test report analysis further along than test automation
The phases end with discovery, because experimenting with use cases is the final step after full integration

questions.explanation: The phases can run in parallel for different use cases; for example, test report analysis may be further along the roadmap than test automation. Early concerns such as fear of job displacement should also be addressed. The other statements contradict the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which competency is MOST important for evaluating AI-generated testware?

options.text: Training transformer models from scratch, so that each tester can rebuild the LLM whenever its answers are wrong
Negotiating contracts with LLM vendors, so that each tester can choose a different model for each prompt
Assessing LLM capabilities, understanding prompt refinement and judging generated output against test expertise
Writing marketing copy, so that generated test reports persuade stakeholders to accept the test results

questions.explanation: Key competencies include assessing LLM capabilities, understanding prompt refinement techniques and evaluating AI-generated testware, combined with domain and test expertise. Training models from scratch, negotiating contracts or writing marketing copy are not the described competencies. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: How do test team members typically progress when building GenAI capabilities, according to the syllabus?

options.text: From fine-tuning LLMs to writing basic prompts, because model training is easier to learn than prompting
From mastering basic prompt creation to using more focused techniques, such as test-specific prompts
From reviewing AI output to ignoring it, because experienced testers can trust generated testware fully
From using approved tools to using personal tools, because advanced testers need more flexible options

questions.explanation: Test team members progress from mastering basic prompt creation to more focused techniques such as test-specific prompts and reusable prompt patterns. The other progressions contradict the syllabus, for example by abandoning review or encouraging shadow AI. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: What new management challenge does the syllabus describe for test managers in AI-enabled organisations?

options.text: Removing traditional testing competencies from the team, because AI literacy replaces the need for test skills
Reducing every test team to a single tester, because GenAI agents perform all other test tasks unsupervised
Coordinating hybrid teams of human testers and GenAI-powered test agents, which needs new leadership skills
Avoiding AI governance frameworks, because governance slows down the adoption of GenAI in test processes

questions.explanation: Test managers will lead human testers and coordinate with GenAI-powered test agents, requiring new skills for managing hybrid teams; they balance human and AI capabilities, establish AI governance and keep both traditional competencies and AI literacy. The other statements contradict the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 53); GenAI-5.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which description fits generative AI on the AI spectrum?

options.text: It uses deep learning techniques to create new content, such as text, images or code, by learning patterns from its training data
It uses search algorithms to find an optimal route through a fixed graph of known test steps and their expected outcomes
It uses symbols and logical rules written by domain experts to reproduce human decisions about known and well-understood situations
It uses manually selected features and labelled historical data to classify new defect reports into predefined categories

questions.explanation: GenAI uses deep learning to create new content by learning and mimicking patterns in training data.
