Rules describe symbolic AI, manually selected features and labelled categories describe classical ML, and search over a fixed graph is not GenAI. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which description of a large language model is consistent with the CT-GenAI syllabus?

options.text: A rule-based expert system that encodes the ISTQB glossary as logical statements and answers questions about it
A small model trained only on an organisation's own requirements, which cannot handle general language tasks
A model based on the generative pre-trained transformer, trained on huge datasets such as books, articles and websites
A database of verified test cases that returns the stored test case whose title is most similar to the tester's request

questions.explanation: LLMs are based on the generative pre-trained transformer deep learning model and trained on very large datasets including books, articles and websites. They are not databases of stored answers or rule-based systems, and compact focused models are SLMs. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 14); GenAI-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which capability distinguishes reasoning LLMs from the instruction-tuned models they build on?

options.text: The ability to retrieve documents from a vector database at runtime before reasoning about a prompt
Structured abilities such as logical inference, multi-step problem solving and chain-of-thought reasoning
The ability to run on low-power devices because they have far fewer parameters than other models
The ability to process images and audio in addition to text through vision-language components

questions.explanation: Reasoning models extend instruction-tuned models by emphasising logical inference, multi-step problem solving and chain-of-thought reasoning. Image and audio processing is multimodality, retrieval is RAG, and running on low-power devices describes small models. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.3 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which input types can a multimodal LLM process, according to the syllabus?

options.text: Structured tables alone, because multimodal models were designed to read spreadsheets of test results
Text alone, because image and sound inputs must first be described in words by the tester before reaching the model
Source code alone, because multimodal models were trained to translate between programming languages
Several modalities such as text, images, sound and video, learned from large and diverse training datasets

questions.explanation: Multimodal LLMs extend the transformer model to process multiple data modalities, including text, images, sound and video, and learn relationships between data types from large, diverse datasets. They are not restricted to text, tables or code. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.1.4 (p. 16); GenAI-1.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which example illustrates the testware creation capability of LLMs?

options.text: Generating a dataset of boundary values and invalid combinations for a registration form
Pointing out conflicting statements between two requirements in the same specification
Drafting defect reports and test reports and keeping a test plan updated as the project evolves
Producing an executable test script from a structured manual test case for a web page

questions.explanation: Testware creation means helping create documents such as test plans, test reports and defect reports and keeping them updated. The other options describe test data generation, test automation support and requirements analysis. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 17); GenAI-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: How can testers refine results iteratively when using an AI chatbot?

options.text: By opening a new session for each prompt so that earlier answers cannot influence later answers
By asking the chatbot to rate its own answers so that no human review of the output is necessary
By increasing the temperature with each prompt until the chatbot produces the same answer every time
By using prompt chaining, where each response informs the next prompt and intermediate outputs are checked

questions.explanation: Through techniques such as prompt chaining, testers can iteratively refine chatbot outputs. Higher temperature increases variability, new sessions lose useful context, and self-rating does not replace human review. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 18); GenAI-1.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which list gives the six components of a structured prompt for software testing?

options.text: Role, persona, temperature, examples, constraints and tokens
Goal, scope, approach, schedule, resources and exit criteria
Role, context, instruction, input data, constraints and output format
Context, instruction, test basis, oracle, coverage and report

questions.explanation: A structured prompt for testing typically includes role, context, instruction, input data, constraints and output format. The other lists mix in model parameters, test concepts or test plan contents. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 21); GenAI-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about combining prompting techniques is consistent with the syllabus?

options.text: Prompting techniques are needed for system prompts alone, so user prompts should never include any examples
Prompt chaining, few-shot prompting and meta prompting can be used together to improve LLM outcomes
Prompting techniques replace the six-part prompt structure, so a structured prompt cannot use any technique
Prompting techniques are mutually exclusive, so each prompt must use exactly one of the three core techniques

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that the core techniques can be used effectively in combination and together with the six-component prompt structure. They are not mutually exclusive and do not replace the structure. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 22); GenAI-2.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Who typically defines the system prompt in a chatbot used for testing, and can its users see it?

options.text: The test manager defines it in the test plan, and it is attached to each defect report the chatbot drafts
Each chatbot user defines it at the start of the session, and it is shown above each of the answers the model gives
The LLM vendor defines it during training, and it is published as part of the model's licence agreement
The developer or tester defines it, and in most interfaces the people using the chatbot cannot see or edit it

questions.explanation: The system prompt is typically defined by the developer or tester to guide the LLM's overall behavior and, in most interfaces, is not visible or editable by the chatbot's user. It is not part of training or a licence, and it is not attached to defect reports. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 23); GenAI-2.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester gives an LLM a requirement for an age input field (valid range 18-65) and asks it to propose which test techniques to apply. Which response would be an appropriate use of GenAI for test analysis?

options.text: Suggesting equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis for the range, to be confirmed by a person
Removing the requirement from the analysis because a numeric range is too simple to need any testing
Approving the requirement on behalf of the product owner so that test design can start without delay
Executing the tests on the live system and reporting which of the boundary values failed in the production environment

questions.explanation: GenAI can suggest relevant test techniques, such as boundary value analysis and equivalence partitioning, based on the type of requirement, and the tester verifies the suggestion. Approving requirements, executing tests in production or dropping requirements are not test analysis tasks for an LLM. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 24); GenAI-2.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester asks an LLM to draft functional test cases from a user story. Which request makes the generated test cases MOST useful for test design?

options.text: Ask for as many test cases as possible, without structure, so that the model explores the feature freely
Ask for test cases written as marketing text, so that stakeholders find the generated output persuasive
Ask for test case titles only, because expected results can be added later by the automation framework
Ask for each test case to include preconditions, inputs, expected results and the acceptance criterion it covers

questions.explanation: When prompted with suitable information, an LLM can suggest preconditions, inputs, expected results and coverage criteria, producing test cases that meet test objectives. Unstructured volume, titles without expected results or marketing text do not support test design. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 25); GenAI-2.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: An API under test changes its request format and endpoints every few sprints. How can GenAI support the automated API regression tests?

options.text: By adapting test scripts to the evolving API specification and generating diverse test data, with checks proportionate to the risk
By freezing the API specification so that the regression tests never need to be updated after a change
By replacing API regression tests with manual exploratory sessions run by the LLM during each sprint
By removing authentication from the API in the test environment so that endpoint changes stop failing

questions.explanation: API regression tests face changing request and response formats, endpoints and authentication; GenAI can adapt scripts to evolving specifications and generate diverse test data, maintaining coverage. Its output must be checked according to the risk. Freezing specifications, replacing tests or removing authentication are not appropriate. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 27); GenAI-2.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A test lead asks GenAI to analyse daily execution data across several weeks. Which outcome reflects test monitoring support described in the syllabus?

options.text: A guarantee that the remaining test cases will pass because the trend of recent results is positive
Identifying trends that predict potential risks and alerting the team about deviations from the test plan
A list of testers to replace, ranked by the number of defects that each tester failed to find in the reporting period
A new test strategy that replaces the organisation's test policy without stakeholder involvement

questions.explanation: GenAI facilitates automation of test monitoring and the analysis of trends to predict potential risks and alert teams to deviations from the plan. It does not replace test policy, guarantee outcomes or rank people. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.4 (p. 28); GenAI-2.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Monthly test summary reports must follow the organisation's template exactly. Which prompting technique is MOST suitable for generating them, and why?

options.text: Prompt chaining, because each sentence of the report must be checked by a human before the next one
Few-shot prompting, because examples of completed reports show the model the required structure and format
Zero-shot prompting, because templates are best followed when the model receives no examples at all
Meta prompting, because the model should design a new template for each monthly report it writes

questions.explanation: Test reporting with a specific output format is a repetitive, constrained-format task for which few-shot prompting is recommended. Designing new templates contradicts the requirement, sentence-by-sentence chaining is disproportionate, and zero-shot gives no pattern to follow. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.2.5 (p. 29); GenAI-2.2.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Generated test cases are technically correct but ignore the bank's domain rules and use terms that conflict with the test basis. Which metric captures this weakness?

options.text: Relevance and contextual fit
Recall of relevant instances
Execution success rate
Diversity of scenarios

questions.explanation: Relevance and contextual fit determines whether output is applicable and appropriate, consistent with the test basis and integrating domain-specific requirements. Execution success rate, time efficiency and diversity measure other aspects. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.1 (p. 31); GenAI-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A prompt with extensive background produces overly detailed test cases that do not generalise to similar features. Which refinement technique is MOST relevant?

options.text: A/B testing of models, because generalisation problems are caused by the vendor rather than by the prompt
Integrating user feedback from customers of the product, because testers cannot judge generated test cases
Adjusting prompt length and specificity, because shorter prompts may yield better generalisation in some cases
Adding more examples of the same feature, because longer prompts generalise better than short ones in each case

questions.explanation: Adjusting prompt length and specificity is a refinement technique: sometimes more context helps, while in other cases shorter prompts yield better generalisation. Longer prompts do not always help, testers' feedback is the relevant input, and the issue lies in the prompt. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 2.3.2 (p. 32); GenAI-2.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why are hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases difficult to fix permanently in LLM output?

options.text: Because LLM vendors publish fixes only once a year, so testers must wait for the next major model version to arrive
Because LLMs are non-deterministic, a defect can seem fixed in one output and reappear in another conversation
Because these defects occur in images alone, so text-based prompts cannot influence their appearance at all
Because testers are not allowed to change prompts, so the same defective output is produced each time

questions.explanation: The non-deterministic behavior of LLMs makes these defects difficult to fix: they may appear fixed for one output but reappear in another conversation with the same LLM. The other explanations are not supported by the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: An LLM orders four test cases for execution. The prompt stated that TC2 creates the customer account needed by TC4, and that TC1 must run last. The LLM's order is TC4, TC2, TC3, TC1. What type of problem is this, and which detection approach fits BEST?

options.text: No problem, because TC1 runs last as required; any order of the remaining three test cases is acceptable
A reasoning error, because TC4 runs before the TC2 it depends on; detect it by logical validation or by executing the order
A hallucination, because TC3 was not mentioned in the prompt; detect it by cross-checking the execution log
A bias, because the order favours odd-numbered test cases; detect it by reviewing coverage of the test strategy

questions.explanation: The order breaks a stated dependency (TC4 needs the account created by TC2), which is a reasoning error; logical validation in review or output testing (running the schedule) reveals it. TC3 was part of the input, there is no systematic skew, and the dependency makes the order wrong. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 35); GenAI-3.1.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which statement about selecting the GenAI model as a mitigation for hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases is consistent with the syllabus?

options.text: Use the smallest model available, because small models cannot produce any reasoning errors at all
Use the same model for every task, because changing models introduces new types of defects
Use the newest model available, because newer models are free from hallucinations and biases
Use an LLM suited to the task at hand, for example one specifically trained for that kind of task

questions.explanation: Selecting the appropriate GenAI model, an LLM specifically trained for the task at hand, is one of the listed mitigations (see also model selection in 5.1.3). No model is free of these defects, and the size or recency of a model alone does not remove them. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What causes the non-deterministic behavior of LLMs that leads to different outputs for the same input?

options.text: The probabilistic sampling processes used during inference
The use of structured prompts with an output format
The random order in which testers type their prompts
The deletion of the training data after each conversation

questions.explanation: The inherent non-deterministic behavior of LLMs arises from the probabilistic sampling processes used during inference, which can produce variations even for identical input. Typing order, deleted training data and structured prompts are not the cause. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.1.4 (p. 37); GenAI-3.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which situation illustrates the privacy concern of unintentional data exposure?

options.text: A generated test report is longer than the template allows, so the test manager has to shorten it manually
A generated test report is delivered late, because the LLM service was busy during the nightly batch run
A generated test report accidentally includes a real customer's account number that appeared in an earlier input
A generated test report uses a different date format, so the dashboard cannot import the report's figures

questions.explanation: Unintentional data exposure occurs when GenAI models generate outputs that accidentally reveal sensitive information. Length, format and timing problems are not privacy concerns. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about request manipulation as an attack vector is correct?

options.text: It extracts confidential training data by overloading the context window with extremely long prompts
It makes the model insert backdoors into generated code, such as calls to a malicious IP address
It introduces data that disrupts the AI's output, such as an image that lures the model into a different context
It changes the model's training data with fake ratings so that future versions behave differently

questions.explanation: Request manipulation introduces data that disrupts the AI's output, for example images that lure it into a different context and provoke hallucinations on acceptance criteria. The other options describe context manipulation, data poisoning and malicious code generation. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 38); GenAI-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How do data protection regulations such as the GDPR relate to using GenAI in testing, according to the syllabus?

options.text: They do not restrict GenAI explicitly, but their safeguards on lawfulness and purpose limitation may limit what can be done
They require LLM vendors to approve each prompt, so testers must wait for approval before sending test data
They apply to production systems alone, so test data used in prompts is outside the scope of the regulation
They prohibit GenAI tools explicitly, so organisations in the EU cannot use LLMs for any software testing tasks

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that data protection regulations like the GDPR do not restrict GenAI applications explicitly but provide safeguards, particularly on lawfulness and limitations on purposes of collection, processing and storage, that may limit what can be done. The other statements are incorrect. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 39); GenAI-3.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why is it difficult to state the exact environmental impact of using GenAI for testing?

options.text: GenAI has no environmental impact, because models run in the cloud rather than on testers' own computers
Accurate data on the environmental impact of GenAI is hard to get, even though its energy use is clearly significant
The impact is a trade secret, so the syllabus forbids testers from estimating the energy use of their tasks
The impact depends on the tester's typing speed, which varies too much between people to be measured

questions.explanation: The syllabus notes that it is hard to get accurate data on the environmental impact of GenAI, but these energy-intensive operations clearly contribute to significant CO2 emissions. The other statements are not supported. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.3.1 (p. 40); GenAI-3.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does the syllabus say test organisations should do about AI regulations, standards and best-practice frameworks?

options.text: Choose one framework and ignore the others, because applying several frameworks creates conflicting duties
Stay updated on how regulations, standards, national laws and frameworks develop, because they continue to evolve
Wait until a single global AI law is published, because current regulations do not apply to test activities
Leave the topic to LLM vendors, because vendors are responsible for meeting standards for each use of their models

questions.explanation: As AI technologies and their regulatory landscapes evolve, test organisations must stay updated on regulations, standards, national laws and best-practice frameworks. The other statements contradict the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 3.4.1 (p. 41); GenAI-3.4.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Where can the LLM in an LLM-powered test infrastructure be hosted, according to the syllabus?

options.text: In the test management tool's database, as a table of prompts and pre-generated answers
On each tester's mobile phone, because test tools must run without a network connection
Inside the system under test, so that the model can observe its behavior during execution
As a third-party service accessed through an API, or as a custom model developed in-house

questions.explanation: The LLM may be hosted as a third-party service accessed via API or as a custom in-house model, generating responses from structured prompts. The other options are not hosting options described in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.1 (p. 44); GenAI-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In the generation step of RAG, how does the LLM produce its response?

options.text: It copies the retrieved chunks word for word, without using any knowledge learned during its pre-training
It ignores the retrieved chunks unless they contain a test case, because only test cases count as context
It combines its existing knowledge with the retrieved information to give more accurate, contextually appropriate output
It retrains itself on the retrieved chunks, so that the next user receives an answer from an updated model

questions.explanation: In the generation step, the retrieved information is fed to the LLM, which generates a response combining its existing knowledge with the newly acquired data, producing more accurate and contextually appropriate output. It does not copy chunks verbatim, ignore context or retrain itself. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.2 (p. 45); GenAI-4.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An LLM-powered agent automatically classifies CI failures and files defect reports. How can the team mitigate the risk of incorrect or misleading results?

options.text: Implement automated verification of the agent's outputs, or use a semi-autonomous agent with human approval for critical actions
Use a higher temperature so that the agent explores more classifications before it decides which report to file
Remove the agent's tools so that it can no longer access the CI system, while keeping the automatic filing of reports
Increase the agent's autonomy so that it files reports faster, because more reports compensate for some incorrect ones

questions.explanation: Agents can produce incorrect or misleading results through hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases; these risks can be mitigated by automated verification of the agents' results or by using semi-autonomous agents for critical tasks. More autonomy, removing tools or raising temperature do not mitigate the risk. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.1.3 (p. 46); GenAI-4.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which list gives challenges of fine-tuning a GenAI model for software testing described in the syllabus?

options.text: Needing high-quality task-specific data, mitigating overfitting, addressing opacity, and managing computational resources
Writing longer system prompts, increasing the temperature, adding seeds, and disabling the context window
Choosing a colour scheme, translating the model card, naming the model, and printing the test reports
Reducing the number of testers, avoiding test environments, removing reviews, and shortening sprints

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists ensuring high-quality, task-specific training data to avoid biased or inaccurate results, mitigating overfitting, addressing opacity in the model's reasoning, and managing significant computational resources. The other lists are unrelated or counterproductive. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 47); GenAI-4.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An organisation wants to use an AI chatbot for test tasks. Which LLMOps considerations are primary for this approach?

options.text: Replacing all test documentation with chatbot transcripts, because conversational output satisfies audit requirements
Managing data privacy and security risks while optimising cost, through an assessed LLM-as-a-Service or in-house open-source deployment
Disabling access controls for the chatbot, because restricting access reduces the number of prompts that testers can send
Building a custom model from scratch and hiring a research team, because chatbots cannot be used with existing language models

questions.explanation: For an AI chatbot, the primary considerations are managing data privacy and security risks while optimising cost, using LLM-as-a-Service if assurances are given or in-house infrastructure with open-source licensed LLMs, after rigorous assessment. The other options are not considerations from the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 48); GenAI-4.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Testers paste defect logs into personal AI tools that their employer has not approved. Which risk of shadow AI does the syllabus link to personal AI tools lacking robust security?

options.text: Information security and data privacy weaknesses that could lead to data breaches
Lower model performance because personal tools cannot process defect logs correctly
Higher energy consumption because personal tools run larger models without security patches
Overfitting of the employer's models because personal tools share their training data

questions.explanation: Personal AI tools may lack robust security, leading to potential data breaches: the information security and data privacy weakness risk of shadow AI. The other claims are not risks listed in the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which consideration for selecting LLMs belongs in a GenAI strategy for testing?

options.text: Selecting the LLM with the most famous brand name, because brand reputation guarantees suitable results for test tasks
Selecting the LLM after the strategy has been implemented, because model choice does not affect test objectives at all
Aligning the selected LLMs with the test objectives, ensuring compatibility with the existing test infrastructure and meeting scalability needs
Selecting a different LLM for each tester, because personal preference is the most reliable predictor of output quality

questions.explanation: Selecting the right LLMs is critical and should be aligned with the test objectives while ensuring compatibility with existing test infrastructure and meeting system scalability requirements. Brand, personal preference or late selection are not the criteria described. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 50); GenAI-5.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which selection criterion asks whether a model can usefully be adapted with domain-specific data to improve accuracy for a given use case?

options.text: Recurring cost
Fine-tuning potential
Model performance
Community and support

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning potential evaluates whether it is possible and useful to fine-tune the LLM or SLM with domain-specific data to improve performance for a use case. The other criteria concern cost, measured performance and support. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: In which adoption phase are practical GenAI use cases identified and prioritised and LLM-powered test infrastructure evaluated?

options.text: Operation and retirement
Discovery and capability building
Utilisation and iteration
Initiation and usage definition

questions.explanation: The initiation and usage definition phase identifies and prioritises practical use cases, evaluates LLM-powered test infrastructure, develops expertise and aligns with organisational needs. Discovery builds awareness and capabilities, and utilisation and iteration integrates GenAI fully. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 51); GenAI-5.1.4 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which skills does the syllabus list as part of successfully integrating GenAI into testing?

options.text: Memorising the training datasets of LLMs, designing GPU chips and writing the vendors' licence agreements
Replacing test techniques with prompts, removing review steps and automating stakeholder approvals
Avoiding all use of LLMs in test design, limiting GenAI to drafting emails and writing meeting minutes
Mastering prompt engineering techniques, understanding model context windows and developing test review methods

questions.explanation: Successful integration requires mastering prompt engineering techniques, understanding model context windows and developing test review methods, combined with domain and test expertise. The other options are unrelated or contradict the syllabus. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which items do communities of practice share to promote continuous improvement in using GenAI for testing?

options.text: Prompt pattern libraries and documented lessons learned from GenAI implementations across projects and domains
Personal login credentials for GenAI tools, so that all members can use the same paid account at once
Unreviewed generated test cases, so that each project can copy them without checking their relevance
Raw production customer data, so that every team can generate realistic test data in the same way

questions.explanation: Communities of practice promote continuous improvement by sharing prompt pattern libraries and documenting lessons learned from GenAI implementations across projects and domains. Sharing credentials, unreviewed testware or production data creates risks. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); GenAI-5.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which statement about test managers in AI-enabled test organisations is consistent with the syllabus?

options.text: They ensure their teams stop using traditional test techniques, because AI literacy makes those competencies obsolete
They ensure their teams use GenAI for all tasks, because balancing human and AI capabilities is no longer necessary
They ensure their teams maintain both traditional testing competencies and AI literacy, and establish AI governance for use cases
They ensure their teams avoid AI governance, because governance frameworks belong to the LLM vendor rather than testing

questions.explanation: Test managers focus on balancing human and AI capabilities, establishing AI governance frameworks for use cases, and ensuring teams maintain both traditional testing competencies and AI literacy. The other statements contradict this. Syllabus reference: CT-GenAI v1.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 53); GenAI-5.2.3 (K1).
